Thus, after that son of a householder had heard of this samādhi from that Buddha, he was filled with joy and exultation; his heart was delighted and satisfied, his wholesome mind arose anew, and he attained the power of the Great Dharma."
Having attained the power of the Dharma, there was no need for him to seek it among gods or humans.

He renounced those seventy thousand women; he renounced four great treasuries, each one yojana in extent, filled with boundless jewels; he renounced eight hundred parks and all the various articles of enjoyment. Then, within the teaching of that Blessed One, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of faith went forth from the home to the homeless life.
"Furthermore, Nandirāja!
When that son of a householder was formerly living at home, he never stepped upon the ground without having spread a cloth over it.

Having gone forth into homelessness, for ten thousand years he likewise did not spread a cloth nor step upon the ground; he neither sat nor lay down during that time, except at the times of eating and using [other requisites]."

For ten thousand years, he did not enter into sleep, nor for even as long as a finger-snap did he ever give rise to conceptualizations of desire, conceptualizations of hatred, or conceptualizations of harm.

During those ten thousand years, no divergent thoughts arose; he exerted himself with diligence solely in accordance with omniscience, attaining the dhāraṇī named "Acquisition of All Words and Sounds," the dhāraṇī named "Comprehension of the Speech of All Buddhas," and the dhāraṇī named "Entry into the Gate of Universal Sound."

When he was thus endowed with such blazing diligence, sixty *nayuta* of devas attended upon that Bodhisattva with devoted service; acting in accordance with his needs, they ensured that his body and mind were at ease, making him capable in his diligent practice.

"Having thus practiced the life of a renunciant with ardent diligence, because he heard this samādhi, he turned his back upon and abandoned the cycle of existence for ninety-nine koṭis of hundreds of thousands of kalpas; he has now encountered seventy thousand Buddhas.
Having practiced the life of a renunciant amidst various circumstances, he has upheld, recited, contemplated, and extensively explained this samādhi to others."

Because he practiced with diligence and acted without negligence, he accomplished this samādhi and realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) within eight kalpas. He attained a dwelling place adorned with such meritorious qualities of a buddha-field, identical to those of that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Vimalamukhacandrasuvikrāntagāmin.

"I now see that in the southern direction, beyond forty-four hundred thousand Buddha-fields, there is a world named Mahāvyūha. Therein he acts as a Buddha, named Subhāṣitārāma-tathāgata, preaching the Dharma, surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose number cannot be exhausted."
"King of Joy!
If those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to swiftly attain mastery in accordance with all dharmas, they should hear, uphold, explain, and contemplate this samādhi."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing again to praise and describe the merits of this samādhi beyond measure so as to cause them to stand out, spoke these verses:
"I recall past eons without bound, As immeasurable as the sands of the Ganges;
At that time there was a wise one, a guide for the world, Whose voice of eloquence was heard in all directions."
In that supreme teaching there was a bhikṣu, a knower of the Dharma and an expounder of the Dharma;
having taught this tranquil samādhi, the prince heard it from him and immediately offered his own robe as a covering, dedicating the merit toward the path of supreme enlightenment.
Furthermore, one beholds boundless guides; having attained the Way, they are named Immeasurable Life.
Whatever wisdom-karma they previously possessed has all been exhausted without remainder, leaving no further retribution;
by hearing this great and wondrous samādhi, those with eloquence shall be endowed with merit.
If, at a later time, there should be those who seek the Way,
they ought to hear of this samādhi, and all evils shall naturally be eliminated.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the Stainless Moon, has expounded this samādhi.
Having heard this, the son of the elder immediately took up the practice of going forth.
For ten thousand years, he contemplated in samādhi;
his feet never trod upon the ground, he wore no clothes, and he did not enter into sleep.
This attainment of supreme enlightenment comes solely from listening together;
one finds no love for the household, nor any desire for wealth or possessions.
Having reached the buddha-fields, one has heard [the Dharma] there in its entirety.
The gateway through which all conditioned phenomena enter is the awakening that follows;
before long, one's mind will be filled therewith, and the chariot of one's intention will likewise be filled.
Such a person swiftly attains bodhi—why, then, do you not exert yourself?
In a future time to come, there will be many who seek awakening;
yet they will lack resources and find no joy, having no desire to practice renunciation.
They will respond with anger, abuse, and threats, insulting and speaking harsh words.
Having each heard this together, they said:
"We shall become Buddhas.
For the sake of desire, we shall endure thousands of manifold sufferings."
A slave to desire, yet saying, "I shall become a Buddha";
having seen the Buddha in a dream, he finds a momentary respite.
Though they may treat others with contempt and pride, they harbor no doubt regarding my awakening.
Having heard this sutra, even if their words do not accord with its meaning,
they will find solace in their own minds and before long shall become Buddhas.
Having heard this truth, and once they have heard it,
they will have no attachments, just like the wind in the sky.
Having thus gone forth, many shall seek awakening.
Out of attachment to their own reputation, they give rise to anger toward one another.
Those who are impoverished and lack merit find joy and pleasure in limited learning;
harboring deceitful hearts toward others, they think, "I have reached the shore of enlightenment."
Having seen the light and attained the realm, sentient beings make offerings;
through even this slight joy, one knows that awakening shall be reached.
Yet that awakening is still far off for those who are envious or deceitful.
I have repeatedly visited the Abode of Wisdom, the Greatly Distant and Most Victorious One.
Having heard this sutra, I know that I shall attain Bodhi;
having seen the land of Amitāyus, it will not be long before I become a Buddha.
Far removed is that Bodhi for one who relies on acquisitions and views;
if the mind is not in accord [with reality], I shall not grant them my prediction.
As for this son of a householder, having already relinquished his accumulation of wealth, [he is likewise predicted].
After having gone forth later, he subsequently frequented the houses of alms-seekers.
Such a samādhi as this— had one heard it previously from Dīpaṃkara and practiced it well— thirsty craving would not arise again.
Though he has shaved his hair and left the household life, he remains bound by the interests of worldly acquaintances;
he carries loads of hemp from the sea while abandoning precious jewels.
If one hears the Middle Way but lacks decisive purity, and possesses no precepts, he is not a renunciant.
One practices the path to enlightenment; therefore, do not be negligent.
If there is a place where [the Dharma] is taught at a later time, one should listen to it.
For the sake of true spiritual friends, one should further act without speaking in dispraise.
One should first pay homage and offer words of praise;
having thus scattered robes, one should further proceed without speaking words of commendation.
Having shed tears and performed the offering, one should then present them to oneself.
Furthermore, amidst the assembly, he speaks of their evil conduct:
they have no affection for their ācāryas and do not respect those who recite nearby;
they disparage one another for minor reasons and harbor malice, envying one another on account of their families.
Relying solely on the merit of others, while failing to contemplate one's own virtue,
one will give rise to fierce and poisonous evil, yet still knows how to provide offerings for the wealthy with flowers,
incense, powdered perfumes, banners, canopies, pennants, and garlands.
If one makes offerings to me with drums and music, one should say:
"I have attained Bodhi.
This is my true offering; having heard of this supreme samādhi, [one should offer it].
One should renounce the gain of knowledge; then practice will be in accord with reality.
Why worship the physical body?
I have already relinquished all aggregates.
One should make offerings to the Dharmakāya, just as Subhūti made his offering;
having renounced even the life one holds dear, always dwelling in an araṇya and recollecting this sūtra,
one should do so for the remainder of one’s life.
"O King of Joy!
I tell you: having practiced and heard this, you must by no means associate with those people, nor form alliances with them through flattery and crookedness."
Regarding this, I do not praise it; among the assembly one should say:
"This is real, this is unreal.
Do not seek to have faith in such things.
Those who dwell amidst sense objects yet desire the Buddha’s bodhi—
because of all such conduct, that bodhi remains very far away.
As for my supernormal powers, behold this great physical strength!
Having already attained these various precepts through my practice,
those who divide their portion between craving and morality are like wild beasts among the assembly;
having abandoned the benefits of social ties, they dwell alone in the araṇya.
It is impossible for me that there should be such a thing; I do not say it is without substance.
In the distant future, at the time of the final age, I entrust this sutra to you.
Amitāyus who emits light, and the Dharma King Acala—
Sixty-three billion Buddhas, along with their entire assemblies, have all been seen by him;
each Teacher has entrusted him, so that in the distant future he may protect the Dharma.
"As for this Seal of Wisdom of the Sūtra, I shall universally uphold it hereafter."
The three thousandfold world-system trembled, and the devas uttered words of praise;
a great rain of flowers fell because they heard this entrustment.
*Observation of the Practice of All Dharmas*, Fascicle Two.
The Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Practice of All Dharmas, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Part Two of Chapter Two: Correspondence with Diligence in Previous Lives.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Rājavikrāmin, together with thirty thousand bodhisattvas, having heard that such as these would occur in the distant future, at the end of the age, when the True Dharma was destroyed after fifty years, shed tears, trembled, their hair stood on end, and sweat broke out from their armpits. They immediately rose from their seats, adjusted their upper robes over one shoulder, knelt with their right knees upon the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and with one voice addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

O World-Honored One! In the distant future, at the end of the age when the True Dharma has vanished for fifty years; when great calamities arrive; when each [era] is in decline; when those who preach the Dharma are oppressed; when omniscience is extinguished; when the pure dharmas are scattered; when there is emptiness and no life-force; when the teachings of the True Dharma are destroyed; when the True Dharma is slandered; when speech characterized by meager wisdom prevails; when idle chatter fills common dwellings; when livelihoods are sought through evil means; when the conduct of each individual is not praised; when the weapons of Māra are rampant; and when great affliction prevails therein—[at such times, we shall protect the Dharma].
We shall renounce our own lives and abandon all the pleasures of acquaintances, wandering like a rhinoceros—whether in a great forest or a small grove—free from all attachment and craving.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s wisdom as extracted from such sūtras—the lineage of the treasury of wisdom that has reached the essence of the Great Dharma, sealed with non-erroneous practice, marked by the dhāraṇī-sūtra that gathers immeasurable roots of goodness, which refutes all external treatises, accords with the awakening to omniscience, upholds the True Dharma, and manifests the happiness of all sentient beings—we shall all copy, read, uphold, and expound them.

"Bhagavān! We are able to endure even the Nairayaṇa hell for the sake of this treasure of samādhi; likewise, we shall not forsake the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, nor shall we forsake unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."

At that time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with King Joy as their leader, with one mind and one voice, uttered this peerless Great Dharma Lion’s Roar before the Buddha, the devas, and the rest of the world, and spoke these verses:
"You should know our minds: Just as we desire to seek awakening, There is no other witness or proof, Except for the Supreme among Men."

He naturally knows our minds; as we seek the supreme wisdom of a Buddha, there is no one else in the three realms of existence who has realized it, like those supreme ones endowed with all virtues who have reached the further shore.
Having already relinquished body and life, with nothing remaining, O supreme among two-legged beings,
one maintains this samādhi during future times of great terror.
Without attachment to the body or concern for life, one completely abandons all kinsmen and their welfare.
Practicing this dustless samādhi, one will encounter no great evils in future times.
Even if for boundless and immeasurable eons one must dwell in the fearsome and bitter sufferings of niraya,
by maintaining this dustless samādhi, I shall endure it at all times.
Such suffering and affliction are boundless; dwelling in niraya, one is distressed and without protection.
By maintaining this stainless samādhi, I shall endure the pain of evil harms.
Within this, I am patient, unwavering and firm in my diligence;
I invite all sentient beings, offering the gift of Dharma without seeking material things—
whether for my own benefit, for the benefit of sentient beings, or for all requisites and possessions whatsoever.
Fame, praise, and blame—I have already endured and relinquished them.
I invite all sentient beings; seeking not material things, I seek only the true Dharma.
I shall extensively expound the Dharma so that all sentient beings may be fully satisfied with the Dharma.
Once purity has been attained, one should practice the conduct of bodhi and bring about vast benefit for the sake of compassion toward sentient beings.
Even if skin, flesh, and bone, as well as marrow and blood, all wither away, [one must persevere].
I shall not be indolent, for I see sentient beings suffering.
Even if my skin, flesh, thin membrane, and blood were to dry up,
I would now break through this body without failing to give rise to even the slightest diligence.
Seeing these sentient beings suffering, amidst the great terrors of disease and affliction,
I shall cause them to cross the ocean of misery and reach the dry land of peace and fearlessness.
Dwelling in an araṇya, having abandoned all attachments, I remain.
Having suffused the perception of loving-kindness everywhere, I bring joy and freedom from distress.
In a secluded forest hermitage, where sounds are few, I dwell;
having abandoned all idle chatter, I do not form bonds of affection with others.
I shall possess a mind of loving-kindness, bestowing happiness upon all sentient beings;
I shall grant them the supreme bliss of the Deathless, so that they may sever their ailments and attain the nature of happiness.
As for those who do not follow this training, or who depart from it contrary to these words—
"I shall practice and abide as taught in this sutra.
We shall no longer follow that which is contrary to what is practiced there;
if it is the conduct of the ordinary person, it is unreal and deviates from the path of suchness."
We shall abide forever within the realm of truthful speech;
as it is taught in this sutra, may we possess that intention;
we shall be heedful, just as the Buddha knows.
Bestowing strength upon sentient beings, I shall go before them.
I shall always remain heedful, just as the Victors know with their omniscient vision;
bestowing strength upon all sentient beings, I shall go before them within the Buddha-wisdom.
I would rather fall into a mass of fire, Or consume poisoned food, Than fail to provide for my spiritual friends, Or fail to speak of the Buddha’s Bodhi.
For the sake of the Dharma I fall into the fire; By eating poisoned food, I enter into suffering.
No longer bound by the interests of knowledge, he does not extensively proclaim unsurpassed bodhi.
Although Māras are immeasurable, they create obstacles for me;
having already abandoned all Māras, I shall become a Cakravartin of the world.
Hundreds of thousands of immeasurable Māras exist therein;
they have all acted as obstacles for me, yet I have already transcended them and am free from affliction. Anuttarajita shall be born in this world.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King of Joy in the Middle uttered this lion’s roar, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, a great light pervaded the world, and all the assemblies scattered flowers from above, offering them into the sky.

Not only one deity, but hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of them raised their voices in praise, and further performed immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of musical instruments, saying these words:

"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva King of Joy will before long proceed to the site of enlightenment; he shall perform the lion’s roar of a Tathāgata, just as the Tathāgatas roar before the world of devas."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke words of praise to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva King of Joy:
"Excellent, excellent, King of Joy!

"You are able to uphold the True Dharma and utter this unsurpassed great lion’s roar—just as you have already uttered such a lion’s roar in the presence of Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River."
“King Priya, listen well, listen well! Attend with right mindfulness and reflection, for I shall explain to you the mass of merit produced by all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who uphold the true Dharma.”
“King Priya, I shall now provide you with a parable; by means of this parable, a wise man among them will understand the meaning of what is said. King Priya!”

Just as there are Buddha-fields equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River in the eastern direction, so too in the southern, western, and northern directions, as well as in the nadir and zenith—thus throughout the ten directions and the intermediate directions—there are Buddha-fields equal in number to the sands of the Ganges; all of these are surrounded by a single city wall.

However, the height of its walls reaches the limit of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); even if such a vast city were filled with mustard seeds, tied at the tip [of a stalk], they would not be leveled out.

At that time, there appeared a certain man who, out of conceptual discrimination, took some mustard seeds in his right hand and cast them into the air above; as soon as they were cast, they vanished without interval.

That great heap of turnip seeds—when, at that time, such winds blow upon that great heap of turnip seeds, shaking, dispersing, and breaking it apart, they cast them into each and every world-system throughout the ten directions; each and every turnip seed falls, never two together, until the entire great heap of turnip seeds has fallen as individual turnip seeds into each and every Buddha-field.
“King of Joy! What do you think?
Is it possible to know the limit of the number of those buddha-fields through skillful means?”
He replied: “No, Blessed One! No, Sugata!”
"Only the Tathāgata knows it in this way.
The Buddha said, "Rājādhirāja!"

Furthermore, if there were one who, with faith and resolve, filled even immeasurable, incalculable, and beyond-counting Buddha-fields with the seven precious jewels and offered them as a gift; yet if there were another bodhisattva who, out of respect for the true Dharma and for the sake of upholding the true Dharma, were able to endure [the hardships] for even a single day and night—then the latter would generate far more merit than the former, for the purpose of causing the true Dharma to abide for a long time.
Why is this? King of Joy!
Once one has received the true Dharma under a single Tathāgata, one has thereby received the true Dharma under all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.
“King Nanda! When various jewels are given away, they are accompanied by outflows and accompanied by grasping.
King Nanda!”
Furthermore, when giving the gift of Dharma, one is without outflows and without grasping, and all sufferings are extinguished.
O King of Joy!
For this reason, you should place your faith and understanding in the gift of Dharma, and not place your faith and understanding in worldly wealth.
"You all should honor me with the offering of the Dharma, not with worldly wealth;
you should revere me with reverence for the Dharma, not with reverence for material things."
Why is this? King of Joy!
The awakening of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, arises from the Dharma; it does not arise from material wealth.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva King of Joy addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We, too, shall revere the True Dharma and not revere wealth.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
It is necessarily by means of the Dharma that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva realizes and awakens to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, not by means of material wealth.
Furthermore, because wealth causes afflictions to increase, while the Dharma causes afflictions to be exhausted, it is therefore transformed.
The Buddha spoke these words of praise to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Pramuditarāja:
“Excellent, excellent! Truly excellent!”
"O King of Joy!
You have spoken these words well:
'The Dharma proceeds because it causes the afflictions to be extinguished.'"
Furthermore, King of Joy!
Listen well, listen well; attend with right mindfulness and I shall speak for you.

Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past upheld the true Dharma, applied themselves diligently to it in accordance with its requirements, and did not begrudge their own bodies or lives, renouncing all pleasures, acquaintances, wealth, profit, and honor, they upheld the true Dharma.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Joyful King said:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
I am most eager to hear this.”
The Buddha said: “Rājavikrīḍita!

In a past age, incalculable kalpas ago—further beyond the countless, the immeasurable, the vast, the unfathomable, and the inconceivable—at that time there appeared in the world a Tathāgata named Vipulaśuddhaghanasuvarṇasamantāsaṃdigdhaprabhātejorāja, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Bhagavān.”
"Furthermore, King of Joy!

That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyī-viśuddha-guru-suvarṇa-samanta-nirvicikitsa-raśmi-tejo-rāja has an immeasurable lifespan; his Buddha-field is adorned with boundless merits; he is surrounded by a retinue of seventy koṭis of hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas, as well as an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas—all of whom have emerged from boundless practices and have entered in accordance with the Dharma-realm."
“King of Joy!

Thus it was that after the Tathāgata Vast Pure Thick Gold Universal Unwavering Light Majestic King had passed away, at a later time when the True Dharma was vanishing, there was a teacher of the Dharma named Boundless Jewel Resounding Voice Pure Conduct Assembly.

Those who preach the Dharma reach the ultimate stage of practice, attain the wisdom of the five supernormal powers, possess mastery over dhāraṇīs, and enjoy uninterrupted eloquence as they accord with and enter the practice of the Dharma.

Entering villages, cities, towns, and royal capitals, they preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; that is to say, they first initiate them by teaching this samādhi of the definitive contemplation of the practice of all dharmas, and they subsequently establish sixty koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

"At that time, many bhikṣus will emerge who resemble those who have entered the path of the heterodox (tīrthika) and are attached to the person (pudgala); they will neither employ this samādhi nor be able to endure it."

Bound by envy and stinginess, they do not permit those bhikṣus who preach the Dharma—namely, those within the territories, villages, towns, marketplaces, and royal capitals governed by the king—to be known, nor do they allow them to enter; they do not speak with them, nor do they count them among their own.
"King of Joy!

At that time, although that Dharma-preacher was driven out of the village, he had no mind of fear or avoidance, no mind of inferiority, no mind of anger or agitation, no mind of thick turbidity, and no mind of defilement; he merely protected the True Dharma in this way."
Having disregarded their own bodies and lives and renounced all wealth, profit, honor, and respect, there was a great king of forests named Dvija-dvija. "Dvija-dvija" refers to a bird:
first, it is born from an egg, which is the first birth; later, it emerges from the shell, which is the second birth.

All those born from eggs should be considered as having two births; because those born from bird eggs are numerous, they alone receive the designation of "twice-born. Shaking their voices and scattering flowers, they proceed toward that place; having arrived, they enter and sit there together with thirty thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas.
As he was wandering within that king of groves, the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Akanistha Heaven came to his presence for the sake of hearing the Dharma.

He preached the Dharma amidst the assembly of the Mahādevas, and there appeared hundreds of thousands of *yojana* of devas and humans filling that space. Within that King of Forests, he preached the Dharma in such and such a manner to the assembly of devas who had the bodies of the Four Great Kings, causing nine million devas to become non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and leading immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sons of gods to realize the wisdom of the Path.
The lords of the Four Great Kings, the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, and the Brahmā lord of the Sahā world will diligently come to serve him, attending to whatever he does;
likewise, there will be thirty thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas who serve that Dharma-preacher.
"O King of Joy!

At that time, there was a king named Many-Folk-Without-Grief-Universal-Desire-Joyful-Sound who emerged upon Jambudvīpa; as a Dharma-king, he ruled with righteousness over the four continents as a wheel-turning monarch, fully endowed with the seven treasures."
"O King of Joy!

Furthermore, that King Many-People-Without-Grief-Universal-Delight-Sound fulfilled his thousand sons; yet they were all born by transformation, emerging from the cross-legged posture without losing right mindfulness.
Within the inner palace, the eighty-four thousand women all practiced the Brahma-faring."
Furthermore, that King Many-Human-Without-Grief-Universal-Wish-for-Joyful-Sound constantly practiced the Brahma-conduct and constantly entered right concentration. "Joyful King!

At that time, the Dharma-preacher Infinite-Virtue-Jewel-Trembling-Sound-Pure-Conduct-Cluster, knowing that the king’s mind had already been perfected through corresponding practices in previous lives and was resolutely set upon the practice for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, manifested himself in the form of a young brahmin (*māṇava*) within the lunar disk during the quiet of the night."

While that king was in his palace surrounded by his inner court ladies, the King [of the Forest] ascended into the sky from that grove—like a king of geese, unattached—and approached the presence of King Many-People-Sorrowless-Universal-Desire-Delightful-Voice. Emerging from the lunar disk, he manifested the form of Brahmā and remained suspended in the air before the king. Having pervaded the palace with radiance, he then spoke these verses for the king:
“O Lord of Men, one who acts contrary to the Dharma will never see his fame or renown increase;
By acting contrary to the Dharma, one finds no happiness; there is no joy in this world for a ruler of men.”
O Lord of the Earth!

You formerly practiced the Dharma as well; having now attained sovereignty over the four continents, you benefit all. Protect the lineage of the Dharma so that it is not severed; O Ruler of Men, follow and protect the practice of the Dharma.
One should follow and protect the true eye of the Dharma; having protected the true Dharma, one rejoices with joy.
Many bhikṣus will emerge who practice without restraint, slandering the Sugata and his enlightenment.
We set forth on the path to the Buddha’s enlightenment, yet we see such beings being abandoned;
if one practices while acting for the sake of these [beings], such beings fall into the evil realms.
In this Jambudvīpa there is a bhikṣu, one who gathers boundless assemblies and makes his voice resound;
he contemplates the meaning and teaches right concentration: that there is no self, no life-principle, and no person (pudgala).
He taught this samādhi of tranquility, by which a bhikṣu drives away all worldly things;
raising his voice within the Pure and Sublime King of Forests, he dwells therein, well-guarding the Dharma.
Abiding in that forest, he dwells in sublime joy; the gods of Akaniṣṭha and other realms have all come.
He teaches this samādhi of tranquility, and many koṭis of gods set out upon the path.
"O King, if you desire wherever you wish to hear the Samādhi of the Ocean of Merit and to bring great benefit to sentient beings,
you should now go to that teacher of the Dharma."
The appearance of a Tathāgata is extremely difficult to encounter; a friend who teaches the True Dharma is likewise very rare.
For sentient beings seeking the Dharma, it is always most difficult; a sovereign who protects the Dharma is the most difficult to find.
"You have sovereignty over this Jambudvīpa; you should uphold the True Dharma.
Always bestowing fearlessness upon those who preach the Dharma, you shall reach such a city where the Dharma is taught."
If the King acts upon what I have said, he shall surely obtain manifold benefits in the future;
he shall bring benefit to sentient beings and, furthermore, attain the bodhi of the Buddha.

"O King Priya! Thus, having performed his inspection in the presence of that king, the Dharma-preacher returned through the path of the sky to enter the lunar disc, and proceeded once more to the place where the King of Forests was."
Having heard this and become aware of it, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; his heart was satisfied and a virtuous intention arose within him.

When that night had passed, together with his full thousand sons, a fourfold army, and a vast multitude of other people, he went to the Great Forest King Vepacitti, the twice-born one who utters a roar and scatters flowers. Having arrived there, he approached the place where the Dharma-preacher was.

At that time, while that Dharma-preacher was extensively expounding this samādhi for the great assembly of devas and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the king, together with his sons and surrounded by his people, beheld both the Dharma-preacher and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they immediately conceived great love, pure faith, and joy.
With pure faith, they prostrated at the feet of that Dharma-preacher and at the feet of that bodhisattva mahāsattva, and then sat down to one side.
Once he has sat down accordingly, that preacher of the Dharma explains this samādhi to him.
Having heard this samādhi, he experiences great exultation, joy, and pure faith.

At that time, that king immediately attained this samādhi; furthermore, among that great multitude, eighty-four thousand sentient beings all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and his thousand sons likewise all attained uninterrupted eloquence.
"O King Priya-rāja!

Thus, with great joy and a heart filled with rapture and exultation, King Viśoka-sarva-prīti-nirghoṣa rose from his seat and offered two priceless robes to cover that bhikṣu who was preaching the Dharma."

The king gave him everything he possessed, including the gift of fearlessness and rest, and served him until the end of his life; according to his needs, he requested to provide him with food and clothing, saying these words: "Bhikṣu!"
"You should descend and enter villages, towns, marketplaces, and royal capitals; with me as your attendant, I shall cause all sentient beings to attain this wisdom.
"O King of Joy! [he said.]
After the king had spoken thus, he prostrated at the feet of that Dharma-preacher and his retinue, and departed to return to his own palace.
"O King Joyful!

At that time, the Dharma-preacher Infinite Merit Jewel-Trembling Sound Pure Conduct-Cluster, having emerged from that Forest King, entered villages, cities, towns, and royal capitals, and set forth to teach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."
That king issued a royal proclamation to all people, saying:
"Let there not be a single person who does not feel affection for this bhikṣu, who does not find joy in him, who does not respect him, or who does not hold him in high esteem."
The thousand sons of that king followed behind that Dharma-preacher, providing continuous protection for the sake of the benefits of the Dharma;
furthermore, thirty thousand other princes and their retinues also served as attendants to that bodhisattva-mahāsattva, following his every action so that they might understand all practices of joy.
“King of Joy!

In this way, for the sake of maturing sentient beings, that Dharma-preacher maintained his own life-span for half an eon by upholding this sutra, and he brought immeasurable sentient beings to full maturity within the Three Vehicles.”

"That king, his son, and their entire retinue, as well as those who served as attendants to that prince and acted as attendants to that bodhisattva, have all therein already resolved upon bodhicitta."

Because they were preceded by the roots of goodness from hearing this samādhi, they all together served sixty *bimbara* of Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, throughout eighty eons. In all those places, they heard this samādhi and, according to their wishes, took up Buddha-fields—some of which reached the state of awakening, and some in which Bodhisattva practices were manifested—for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
“King Priya! During that period, there was a teacher of the Dharma named Anantaguṇaratnanirghoṣaviśuddhacaryāsaṃcaya. Do you harbor a doubt in your mind, thinking:
‘Is it someone else?’”
"Do not view it in such a way. Why is this?
It was the Tathāgata Amitāyus who preached the Dharma during that period."
"Furthermore, King Priya!
During that period, there was a king named Bahujanāśoka-sarvābhiprāyapriyaghoṣa. Do you think he was someone else? [No, he was not.]”
"Do not view it in this way.
Why? Because it is the Tathāgata Acalā."
"Furthermore, King Priya!
Regarding those thousand sons of that king at that time, do you think they were anyone else?
[They were none other than yourselves. "
"Do not view it in such a way. Why is this?
These are the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within this Bhadrakalpa—the ones who shall appear as the thousand Buddhas during this Great Bhadrakalpa."
"Furthermore, King of Joy!

At that time, during that season, there were thirty thousand bodhisattva friends belonging to that Dharma-preacher, the Pure Conduct Assembly whose voice resounds with boundless merit-jewels; they followed him in continuous succession, surrounding him. Do you harbor any doubt in your mind, thinking: 'Are these others?'"
"Do not view it in this way. Why is that?
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize unexcelled perfect enlightenment within a single kalpa."
“King of Joy!

In this way, by embracing the true Dharma and diligently applying oneself to it, a bodhisattva mahāsattva brings benefit to immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings and swiftly attains this samādhi.”
“King of Joy!

For that reason, whether I am present before you or have entered parinirvāṇa, you should receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, and extensively expound this samādhi for others; thus you shall swiftly shatter the armies of Māra.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause this meaning to rise up in immeasurable height, spoke again in verse:
“If one were to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings for thousands of nayutas of inconceivable eons,
the measure of that merit would not equal even a fraction of the merit gained when such a mind as this gives rise to the cause of bodhi.”
If all sentient beings throughout the ten directions were to become supreme Pratyekabuddhas,
and one were to make offerings to them for a thousand koṭis of eons with a pure mind, constantly providing them with joy;
yet, once the aspiration for this Bodhi has arisen, one says:
"I shall attain the state of the supreme among bipeds"—
this single verse of this samādhi, when upheld, surpasses all other merit.
Even if those sentient beings were to encounter Buddhas throughout the world for a thousand koṭis of kalpas and make offerings to them, [it would not equal the merit of upholding this verse].
Even that [previous merit] cannot be compared to the merit of one who, with a single-minded resolve,

generates the supreme bodhicitta; nor does the merit of the four-line verse of this samādhi equal the merit of one who protects the Buddha-dharma in such a way as those guardians of the True Dharma do.
If, among the sentient beings in this world, there were one who transformed others toward bodhi,
and another who, upon hearing [this teaching], felt no fear regarding the path that cannot be grasped— the latter’s merit would be superior.
If there were a bodhisattva who practiced giving for as many koṭis of kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
filling the world-systems with all kinds of precious jewels, yet did not hear of this samādhi;
whereas if someone were to hear of this concentration and a wise person were to uphold even a single four-line verse of it—
One who has gathered a vast mass of merit does not bestow it even over many billions of eons;
yet one who protects the supreme state of awakening may do so.
This inconceivable, stainless concentration cannot be fully described in words, except for those who possess the merit to grasp it.
At the time of death, one shall see many Buddhas; One shall never forget whatever mindfulness one possesses therein.
Regarding the buddha-fields one wishes to travel to, one should write down and uphold this samādhi.

The physical bliss one possesses is like the bliss of the mind; having been born in the heavens and having met with holy beings, one shall never again experience the suffering that has not yet been experienced, because of rejoicing in the King of Samādhis.

The gateways of entry numbering a thousand nayutas, permitted by the Victorious One of boundless radiance—I have now abided in these as taught by the One of Supreme Power; it is through this samādhi alone that awakening is attained.

As one attains eloquence through the gateway of dhāraṇī, and as one attains samādhi like the supernormal powers, that which is realized by wisdom is noble and untainted; thus one expounds this samādhi.
In all the lands where the wise are born, they shall behold the Buddhas before them, hear their teachings, and receive and uphold them;
this is due to the recitation and cultivation of this samādhi.
If they attain a handsome form with no deficient faculties, and the thirty-two marks of a hundredfold merit, it is through this very concentration.
Sentient beings, having seen this, attain great joy; through this samādhi, they engage in recitation and study.
With wise and beautiful voices that delight the mind, they reach the shore of the sixty kinds of vocal qualities;
grasping the Buddha’s voice, they purify sentient beings, for by hearing praise of this samādhi as "excellent," they are transformed.
They shall attain wisdom that is well-beneficial, and they shall also attain knowledge free from turbidity;
furthermore, they shall know the minds of all sentient beings, if they uphold this tranquil samādhi.
There is no gateway of sound through which they enter, nor do they give rise to discursive speech therein.
One attains skillfulness regarding all sounds by reciting the *Vimala-samādhi*;
one becomes free from carelessness, shame, and fear, and further attains joy and exultation.
One’s delight never diminishes by extensively expounding this samādhi.
What I now perceive is as if it were in my hand; you all should now cultivate a right mind.
You are my children; follow my instruction, and by practicing this samādhi, you shall surely attain it.
I have this much that I can say; you who practice with a pure mind should strive while I am still present, lest you be tormented by regret at a later time.

Thus, in the *Samādhi of the Boundless Practice of All Dharmas*, the second chapter, "Praising the Correspondence with Diligence in Previous Lives," is concluded. Chapter Three: The Chapter on Prophecy (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*). Part One of the *Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Practice of All Dharmas*. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Rājavikrāmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is marvelous, Bhagavān!"
Most excellent and rare, Sugata!
Even unto the Tathāgata, you have proclaimed and praised all the merits of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who uphold the true Dharma.
“World-Honored One!
With what dharmas fully endowed does a bodhisattva attain this samādhi?
The Buddha said:
“King of Joy!
A bodhisattva who is fully endowed with one dharma attains this samādhi. What is that one?
“King of Joy!
In this regard, a bodhisattva dwells with firm vows within *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Should anyone there attempt to destroy them, mock them in their presence, disparage them to others, contend with them, revile them in anger, or reproach them, they give rise to no resentment, no aversion, and no harbored grudge toward such persons.”
He dwells observing his own mind as follows:

"When I resolved upon the bodhicitta, no one requested me—neither devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, kinnaras, gandharvas, mahoragas, nor humans or non-humans—and there was not even a single other person in the world who requested me; it was solely through my own mind’s reflection that I gave rise to the thought of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
However, when such thoughts arise in me, all Buddhas are aware of them.
I must not act in this way:

whether I am defeated by another’s mastery over me, or if they mock me in my presence, or revile me, or rebuke me, or deceive me, or treat me with derisive familiarity, or speak words of harm, or strike me to terrify me into abandoning bodhicitta or abandoning sentient beings; or if I should give rise to a narrow-minded intent, or the mind of a śrāvaka, or the mind of a pratyekabuddha—I would then be deceiving the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
"If this mind has given rise to bodhicitta, I must now abide by firm and steadfast vows.
Once that thought has arisen, he shall never abandon it until he sits at the seat of enlightenment.
"King of Joy!
This is the one dharma by which a bodhisattva, being fully endowed with it, attains this samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to make this meaning universally clear in its full extent, further spoke these verses:
"The wise constantly give rise to firm vows, seeking the unsurpassed, great Bodhi;
I shall not grow weary in the interim, practicing the path to enlightenment with an untiring mind."
If one is mocked, contradicted, or disputed; if reviled, scolded, or not honored—if the mind complies with such circumstances and comforts itself, no anger or resentment will arise therein.
"When my bodhicitta arose, it was not gods or nāgas who requested it of me;
rather, I gave rise to compassion for all sentient beings because my mind was directed toward awakening."
If I were now to harbor a small mind, I would be deceiving all the World-Honored Ones;
I shall advance resolutely without weariness, guarding my vow to become a Buddha.
For such a practitioner of great renown, this samādhi will manifest;
with the bodhicitta firmly established as the foundation, the attainment of the awakening of practice is not difficult.
“King of Joy!
Furthermore, by being fully endowed with two other dharmas, a bodhisattva attains this samādhi. What are these two?
"Acting according to what one says, practicing all pure dharmas (śukladharma) without weariness.
'King of Joy! Among these, what is meant by acting according to what one says?'"
When this bodhisattva hears that there are bodhisattva practices and hears that the Buddha-dharma is universally complete, they take this up and think:
"I too shall practice this.
Having practiced the bodhisattva path, they shall thereby awaken to the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.
He acts exactly as he speaks; his conduct is perfected and his practice is pure—this is what it means to act in accordance with one's words.
"What is meant by not being weary among all wholesome deeds?"
This bodhisattva reflects:
"Omniscience is immeasurable; likewise, sentient beings are immeasurable.

To accomplish their welfare, it is not possible for them to fulfill that immeasurable omniscience or to accomplish the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings through meager roots of virtue or meager practices."
When he gives rise to such wholesome states, he dedicates those immeasurable dedications in a manner that is like the great ocean; he never tires of seeking out what he has heard.
"O King of Joy!
These are the two dharmas, fully possessed by which a bodhisattva attains this samādhi.
Within that, it further says these words:
“As they speak, so they act; there is nothing in them that does not accord with their words.
They do not even speak of anything different from this.
Those Bodhisattvas act according to their speech; having heard such characteristics and conduct, they practice accordingly.”
The wise act exactly as they speak; they attain this meditative concentration and the qualities of a Buddha.
Never weary of pure dharmas, they never experience satiety;
such is their immeasurable awakening and their nature of immeasurable merit.
Furthermore, one never tires of or finds satisfaction in pure dharmas; the mind is always insatiable like the ocean.
Regarding the immeasurable and boundless realm of sentient beings, one must not have a narrow mind that seeks satisfaction.
Acting exactly as one speaks, and not wearying of the Dharma while seeking within it—
when training in accordance with these two dharmas, one attains this concentration and the qualities of a Buddha.
“King of Joy!
Furthermore, by being fully endowed with three other dharmas, a bodhisattva attains this samādhi.
What are these three?
This bodhisattva achieves three kinds of prohibitive precepts; what are the three?
They are the precepts of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore, they are free from the three kinds of afflictive burning heat; what are the three?
He refers to the burning heat of greed, the burning heat of hatred, and the burning heat of delusion;
as well as practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) without relying on the three realms.
When these three factors are fully present, the bodhisattva attains this samādhi.
Furthermore, it is said therein:
"Restraining the three spheres— body, speech, and mind—
and having stilled the three afflictions, one does not rely upon the triple world."
"Restraining body, speech, and mind, With the three types of afflictions stilled within the mind,
And not making reliance upon the three realms— For these reasons, one swiftly attains samādhi."
“King of Joy!
Furthermore, by being fully endowed with four other dharmas, a bodhisattva attains this samādhi. What are these four?
He is said to know phenomena produced from causes.
Having known those causes and having known the phenomena produced from causes, he abandons those causes and does not cling to the phenomena produced from causes.
When his knowledge is thus complete, the bodhisattva does not perceive a single phenomenon that is not produced from causes; he reflects in this way:
"If those phenomena arise through causes and conditions, they are empty by nature and do not arise.
Furthermore, having become thus endowed with wisdom, he does not give rise to ignorance, but teaches the Dharma to sentient beings so as to extinguish ignorance;

he does not give rise to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), but teaches the Dharma to sentient beings so that they may understand volitional formations; and likewise, up to not giving rise to old age and death, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings so that they may transcend old age and death.
"O King of Joy!
A bodhisattva who is fully endowed with these four dharmas attains this samādhi.
Within that, it further says:
“Having understood dependent origination, and likewise having understood that which arises from causes,
one then has no views such as annihilationism or eternalism;
and one thoroughly understands both the cause, as well as its characteristics and its intrinsic nature.”
If phenomena belong to causes, wisdom does not cling to them;
that which is produced by causes and conditions, if it exists as a reality, is empty.
If wisdom operates within that [emptiness], one attains samādhi.
Having universally understood ignorance, all volitional formations do not arise;
as they are known, so they are taught, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
If these four dharmas exist, then the Bodhisattvas, those most excellent ones, [will attain their goal].
"It is not difficult for him to attain this samādhi praised by the Buddha.
'O King of Joy!
Furthermore, when another five dharmas are fully possessed, a bodhisattva attains this samādhi.'"
What are these five?
O King of Joy!
They are that a bodhisattva knows how to act, knows how to harmonize, knows the gateways, knows the practices, and knows the path.
"In this regard, what is 'action'? That which is called action is:
to maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, to relinquish various conceptualizations, and to regard all sentient beings with a single-flavored compassion—this is called action."
"In this regard, what is 'union' (saṃyoga)?

If one knows that the ripening of retribution within the body is such that the wholesome karma performed is dedicated toward Bodhi, and one does not come into contact with it therein, this is called 'union'."
"In this regard, what is the gate?

That which is called a 'gate' refers to the gate of emptiness and the gate of ambrosia—according to the Sanskrit original, it is called 'the immortal' (*amṛta*), though its traditional meaning has long been 'ambrosia' (*amṛta*). Within this, there is also no dependence on another; this is what is called a gate."
"In this regard, what is 'practice' (caryā)?

It refers to the practice of emptiness, the practice of solitude, the practice of suchness, and the practice of the universal purity of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; this is called practice."
"Among these, what is the path?
It is that which is free from the activity of 'I' and the activity of 'mine'; this noble right view is called the path.
O King of Joy!
"When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these five dharmas, they attain this samādhi.
Within that, it further says:
"Among sentient beings with equal minds, they act in such a manner."
Furthermore, believing that the retribution of karma ripens, one then accords with this unsurpassed [path].
Having universally abandoned all non-path and minor dharmas, one seeks the wholesome dharmas without ceasing or desisting;
all are dedicated toward bodhi, yet there is nothing touched within bodhi.
"Knowing the gates of liberation—namely emptiness and signlessness—and likewise not forming any aspiration: this is the unsurpassed gate.
Being skillful regarding all phenomena, one never relies upon any phenomena."
Abiding alone in accord with the realm of non-arising, where "I" and "mine" do not arise;
for the wise who dwell constantly within the fourfold application, effort, cultivation, and the path—
enlightenment is not difficult to attain, let alone this tranquil samādhi!
"King of Joy!
Furthermore, by being fully endowed with six other dharmas, a bodhisattva attains this samādhi. What are these six?

He is said to know the eye and to know the intrinsic nature of the eye. Having known the eye and having known the intrinsic nature of the eye, he has no attachment or obstruction regarding forms that are pleasing to the mind or those that are not pleasing to the mind;

he reaches a state of equanimity, and this eye-faculty is not scorched by these forms. Likewise, he knows the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and he knows the intrinsic nature of the mind. Having known the mind and having known the intrinsic nature of the mind, he has no attachment or obstruction regarding mental phenomena (*dharma*) that are pleasing to the mind or those that are not pleasing to the mind; he reaches a state of equanimity, and this mind-faculty is not scorched by these mental phenomena.
"O King of Joy!
A bodhisattva who is fully endowed with these six dharmas attains this samādhi.
Within that, it further says:
"Knowing the self-nature of the eye is not a self-nature as a self-nature;
one is not obstructed within forms, whether they be empty or impure.
Reaching equanimity amidst forms, one has no defilement of desire."
Having known the essence of the fundamental nature, there is no burning for them;
likewise, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—
having known their own nature, they do not cling to any phenomena.
Restraining the six sense objects, preventing them from wandering outward,
one becomes fully endowed with the wisdom of intrinsic nature— neither desiring nor free from desire.
With such supreme wisdom and equanimity, this is the victorious Bodhisattva.
"It is not difficult for him to attain this samādhi praised by the Buddha.
'O King of Joy!
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva is fully endowed with another seven dharmas, he attains this samādhi.'"
What are these seven? They are:
being without guile, being straightforward, desiring the Dharma, seeking the Dharma, examining the Dharma, expounding the Dharma, and practicing the Dharma.
"O King of Joy!
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these seven dharmas, they attain this samādhi.
Within that, it further says:
"Free from flattery and crookedness, always upright, Without divergent speech and with no discrepancy between thought and deed, As one intends, so one speaks;
the wise person delights in this for themselves and shares it with others."
Abiding in accordance with the Dharma and practicing the Dharma, one never regards sound as supreme;
by thus diligently applying oneself, one attains meditative concentration and swiftly touches the unsurpassed Great Bodhi.
He who possesses the dharma of desire for greatness and fame, seeking to hear it without ever being satiated,
observes with right mindfulness according to what he has heard, and in turn explains it extensively for the sake of many people.
"King of Joy!
Furthermore, by being fully endowed with eight other dharmas, a bodhisattva attains this samādhi.
What are these eight?

It is because his aggregate of ethical discipline is universally pure; because he is free from all attachments; because he always possesses the mind of one who has gone forth; because he delights in dwelling in secluded places; because he does not seek various gains and offerings; because he does not cherish body or mind; because his faith and understanding are lofty; and because he maintains an even mind toward the pleasant and the unpleasant.
"O King of Joy!
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these eight dharmas, they attain this samādhi.
Within that, it further says:
“Having purified the aggregate of precepts and dwelling well within that purity,
one who has abandoned all attachments goes forth in the supreme teaching.
A bhikṣu in the teaching of the Sugata should renounce gain and honor.”
Yet seeking to abide in this tranquility—this concentration is most difficult to perceive.
If one contemplates and cultivates this supreme practice, there will be no distinction between the pleasant and the unpleasant;
by embracing the eight worldly dharmas and proceeding accordingly, one attains this sublime samādhi.
"O King of Joy!
Furthermore, by being fully endowed with another nine dharmas, a bodhisattva attains this samādhi.
What are these nine?
“O King of Joy!

This refers to that bodhisattva who abandons the nine matters of anger, transcends the nine abodes of sentient beings, accomplishes the nine successive meditative attainments, passes beyond the eight inverted errors, enters the eightfold right path, leaves behind the eight unfavorable conditions, realizes the eight liberations, knows the seven stations of consciousness, and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment.”
"O King of Joy!
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with these nine dharmas, they attain this samādhi.
Within that [text], it further says:
"The nine abodes of sentient beings—within these, sentient beings rely [on them].
Because they have severed and abandoned all views, they have no further questions regarding reliance.
Having severed and abandoned the eight unfavorable conditions (akṣaṇas) and having already realized the eight liberations,"
Regarding the seven stations of consciousness, the wise one knows them all through right mindfulness.
Cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, they sever all conceptualization and uproot afflictions.
Thus, through diligent application, they attain concentration and swiftly touch supreme enlightenment.
“King of Joy!
Furthermore, by being fully endowed with another ten dharmas, a bodhisattva attains this samādhi. What are these ten?

It is said that this consists of: relinquishing all that one possesses; enduring and purely upholding the immeasurable cycles of saṃsāra; fulfilling supramundane wisdom; maintaining great loving-kindness toward sentient beings without perceiving them as discrete entities; retaining all that has been heard through extensive learning; transcending all conceptual designations through great compassion; employing skillful means without seeking personal pleasures; universally recollecting all Buddhas; not forgetting these ten paths of wholesome action even in dreams; and teaching the Dharma based on the bodhicitta without envying other vehicles.
"O King of Joy!
When these ten dharmas are fully possessed, a bodhisattva attains this samādhi.
Within that, it further says these words:
"Having renounced all possessions with joy, possessing patience, gentle speech, and a straightforward mind, practicing for billions of eons without deficiency—they quickly attain this samādhi.
Those with wisdom are free from afflictions; those with a compassionate heart have no worldly desires."
Those who embrace all that they have heard without forgetting, and thereby attain this tranquil samādhi;
those who feel compassion for all sentient beings and refrain from frivolous discourse, and who do not cling to pleasure despite their skillful means;
those who universally keep all Buddhas in mind with right mindfulness—they shall attain this tranquil samādhi.
They protect all ten wholesome paths, keeping them entirely pure, never losing them even in their dreams;
their minds remain focused on the conduct leading to Bodhi, never envying the Lesser Vehicle.
If one possesses such a most excellent Dharma, it will not be difficult to attain among all the Buddha-teachings;
one will swiftly destroy the hosts of Māra and shall touch the most excellent, pure Bodhi.
Furthermore, when the Blessed One spoke this Dharma-text, seventy thousand sentient beings attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding dharmas, being free from dust and defilement;
seven thousand sentient beings all resolved upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and were all granted the prediction of non-retrogression;
and thirty thousand bodhisattvas attained patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, so that they might protect the city of the Dharma at a later time.
The roots of goodness of immeasurable sentient beings were brought to fulfillment.
This trichiliocosm shook in six ways, a great light pervaded the world, the three evil realms were stilled, and all sentient beings beheld the Tathāgata before them.
The World-Honored One again emitted light from his body; by means of this light, immeasurable and innumerable worlds were filled with a great radiance.

When that light reached the bodies of those sentient beings, they all attained right mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, became endowed with happiness, and were freed from their feverish afflictions.

The light of that Blessed One, throughout the ten directions, was adorned with boundless jewels—not merely a hundred thousand kinds of colors—but from places where hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lotuses with a hundred petals had emerged, there appeared within each lotus an image resembling the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Blessed One.

However, those images resembling the Tathāgata appeared seated upright within those lotuses. Within the lotus calyxes of all those lotuses, there were figures resembling the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Priyadarśana; having placed their right knees upon the lotus calyxes, they likewise asked about this samādhi, and those Tathāgatas likewise extensively expounded this samādhi. Each and every Tathāgata awakened and brought to maturity immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Joyful King, saying: “Joyful King!

Do you see throughout the ten directions those who resemble these immeasurable and innumerable Tathāgatas seated upon lotus flowers, as well as those who resemble the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Joyful King?”
He replied: "I have seen them, Blessed One! I have seen them, Sugata!"
"But I do not know their number.
The Buddha said, "King Priya!"

One might be able to grasp a number equal to the sands of the Ganges, yet one cannot know the number of those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; all such Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, whom you have seen—just as they are, so too even Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas like yourself cannot know their number.
At that time, having withdrawn his marvelous supernormal powers, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Joyful King, saying:
"Joyful King! What do you think?"
"Does the Tathāgata go from this buddha-field to another place?
Does he move from his seat?
Or do you also go to another place?"
He replied: "No, Blessed One! No, Sugata!"
The Buddha said: “King Priya!

By this cause and condition, you should know that all dharmas are suchness (tathatā). They arise from the conceptualization of the marks of birth, activity, and abiding; they neither come nor go, being just as they are desired and just as they are acted upon.”
Because they are without a master, you should see them all as empty and disintegrated.
"O King of Joy!

Therefore, you should have faith and understanding in all phenomena; you should view them as being like a mirage, a dream, a reflection, an echo, the moon in water, or a flash of lightning and a bubble. You should train yourselves in this way."
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva who possesses profound faith and understanding shall attain this samādhi.
*The Sūtra on Contemplating the Practice of All Dharmas*, Scroll Three.
