Chapter Three: The Bestowal of Prophecies, Part Two.
In this regard, the Blessed One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Rājavikrāmin, saying: "Rājavikrāmin!

Suppose a bodhisattva, relying on sentient beings, practices giving, guards the precepts, maintains patience, exerts diligence, enters meditative concentration, and cultivates wisdom for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; yet, Rājavikrāmin, if another person were to hear this Dharma-gate and give rise to even a single thought of faith, the latter would generate far more merit than the former."

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva has faith and understanding that all phenomena are selfless, this merit will surpass that mass of merit born from [the aforementioned practices], and they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Why is this?
O King of Joy!

In the past, beyond incalculable eons, further beyond countless, vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable [eons], at that time and in that season, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata named Ratnarcis-cakravartin-rāja, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of persons, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Bhagavān. His world was named Saratna, and his eon was named Abhigamana.
"Furthermore, King Priya!

At that time and in that era, the world-system called Ratnavatī belonging to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnatejorājacakravartin, was wealthy, abundant, and prosperous; it was exceedingly delightful and teeming with many people."

It is as level as the palm of a hand, free from tiles and pebbles, and abundant with gold and silver; it is as soft to the touch as kācilindika cloth, with the eightfold paths intersecting one another.
Within the expanse of this great earth, there naturally arise lotuses of pure blue vaidūrya and jāmbūnada gold, as large as chariot wheels, exquisite in fragrance and color.
"That world is vast, consisting of sixty-four hundred thousand *koṭis* of continents; within each set of four continents, there are sixty-four hundred thousand cities."

Those great cities were each thirty-two yojanas in circumference; all were surrounded by walls made of the seven precious substances and were inhabited by many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of sentient beings.

Each of these great cities is surrounded by twelve thousand villages, garrisons, and market towns; within each of those great cities, there are five hundred pleasure gardens, adorned and graced by various flowers, fruits, fragrances, and jewel trees.

Within each of those gardens, there are thirty-two lotus ponds, filled to the brim with water possessing the eight excellent qualities; they are strewn with golden sand and surrounded by jeweled railings, interspersed with lapis lazuli and crystal, and within them grow precious *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers.

Within those blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and water lilies, flocks of geese, swans, cormorants, peacocks, ruddy sheldrakes, kalaviṅkas, and jīvañjīvakas dwell; having settled there, each utters its own song.
“O King of Joy!

At that time, in that era, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Ratnarcis-tejorāja, had a garden named Priyadarśana. Within it was a place where the World-Honored One dwelt and the king governed, called Candravatī. There he resided together with seventy-two koṭis of śrāvakas and eighty-four koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive.”

"Rājavikrīḍita! In the realm governed by King Candra, there are seventy-two koṭis of inhabited places for sentient beings; throughout all those locations, the Eightfold Path runs through them, interconnecting them."
"Furthermore, King Priya!

There was a realm governed by King Candra, sixty-four yojanas in extent, with sevenfold walls and railings made of the seven precious substances, featuring various jeweled gates and pillars, as well as rows of tala trees everywhere draped with nets of bells."
"Furthermore, King Priya!

At that time and at that juncture, in the central region governed by the Moon King, there was a king named Ratnacandra who ruled as a universal monarch over the four thousand continents, acting as a Dharma-practicing Dharma-king."
Furthermore, King Priya!

That King Ratnacandra constructed a palace within the realm governed by King Candrasūrya—a palace composed of the seven precious gems, four *yojanas* in circumference, with sevenfold walls, and further surrounded by hanging networks of bells made of the seven precious gems, as well as canopies of *maṇi* jewels covering its summit.
Within that palace, there are four great gardens in the four directions:
the first is named Variegated Chariots, the second Constantly Blooming Flowers, the third Delightful to Behold, and the fourth Righteous Conduct and Joy.

“In that great garden there grow various kinds of trees—namely, jewel trees, flower trees, incense trees, fruit trees, garland trees, clothing trees, music trees, puṣya trees, moonlight trees, and sun-flame trees.”

Within that great garden, each [quarter] has four large lotus ponds filled everywhere with sandalwood-scented water. They are surrounded by jeweled railings, strewn with Jāmbūnada gold dust and various precious gems, and their surfaces are covered with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, while ruddy sheldrakes call out in harmony.
"Furthermore, King Priya!
That King Ratnacandra had forty-two thousand women, resembling celestial maidens; among them was one chief queen named Bhadrā, whose complexion was more radiant than that of the gods."
"Furthermore, King Priyarāja!

That King Ratnacandra had twelve thousand sons, whose forms and colors were exquisite; those who saw them felt faith and affection for them. They were fully endowed with the most supreme and pure physical perfection, their bodies universally adorned with the twenty-eight marks of a great man."

“King Joyful! At that time, King Jewel Moon went out to the Garden of Delightful Sight to sport and enjoy himself. A chief celestial consort named Endowed with Fortune suddenly gave birth to a boy through miraculous transformation; he sat cross-legged, his form and color were most excellent and sublime, inspiring faith and love in all who saw him, and he was fully endowed with the twenty-eight marks of a great man.”
When he was born, he spoke thus:
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, without abiding, and without stability; they are subject to the nature of perversion and proceed in continuous succession."
He spoke this verse:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, unstable, without rest, and lack solidity; they are subject to change.
Yet ordinary people and the small-minded regard them as permanent and stable, due to their craving and negligence and lack of right mindfulness."
Whether among devas or humans, according to whatever desires they have, all are of the nature of impermanence and exhaustion;
there has never been satiety regarding desire, for unstable desire is suffering and the very root of suffering.
Renowned as Jewel-Light, supreme among men, he taught the stainless and unconditioned Dharma;
therein all the sense-faculties are stilled without remainder, as is the bliss of Bodhi, the noble and untainted.
Venerable One, please now listen to these words of mine: the appearance of a Tathāgata is rare and difficult to encounter;
we should go together to the presence of the Sugata, for the celestial radiance of the Victorious One surpasses that of the gods.
"O King of Joy! At that time, King Ratnacandra addressed the youth again in verse:
'Are you a deva, a nāga, or a yakṣa spirit?'
"O youth! Explain this meaning for me.
As soon as you were born, you spoke these words, praising the Buddha-dharma."
From where did you die to come here? Tell me, what is your name?
Your light pervades this entire grove; O one of supreme virtue and majestic power, you shine forth brilliantly.
The youth replied: "In the eastern direction, there is a supreme man named Śikhin, the Guide of the Śibis;
I have come here from there after dying in that place, desiring to see the Dharma King Prabhāsa."
I am named Dharmodgata; know this well. Now I set forth on the path toward supreme Buddha-wisdom.
If you, O Honored One, likewise wish to hear the Dharma, it is fitting that we go together to the presence of the Sugata.

"Joyful King! At that time, King Ratnacandra, together with the youth Dharmottara and his women, surrounded by the princes and a vast multitude of people, proceeded in front toward the park called Priyadarśana to go before that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnarcis-tejorāja."
Having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.
That great multitude of people likewise prostrated at the feet of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaprabhāsavikramacakravartin, and withdrew to stand to one side.
“After the youth Dharmodgata had prostrated at the feet of that Blessed One and kissed them, he spoke these words:
‘Blessed One! The Tathāgata Merupradīpa sends his greetings, saying:’”
“Does the Blessed One have little illness and little affliction? Is his daily life light and easy, and does he experience vigor and comfort in his movements?
Having spoken thus, the youth Dharmottara stood before that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnaprabhāsatejorāja, and addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“O inconceivable, supreme Arhat! O Unsurpassed Honored One!”
The Most Victorious One who proclaims the practice of non-contention, Who delivers immeasurable multitudes of sentient beings— To the Lord of Men seated upon his throne, I now pay homage.

He is the Teaching King of this trichiliocosm; The World-Honored One is able to bestow the treasure of the Dharma, Extensively expounding for others the jewel-treasury of the Dharma-store, And shattering the armies of the Māra-king and the rākṣasas.
Among the assembly, you shine like the light of the moon, extensively teaching the path for crossing to the other shore;
O Teacher, O Sugata, you who possess the five faculties, the five powers, and the five eyes!
I take refuge in the Teacher, who has exhausted all afflictions; Who turns the wheel of Dharma within this realm as a universal monarch;
Who has removed the three stains like a clear eye, And whose stainless eye purifies the entire world.
Māhoragas and all sentient beings—there is none among them who does not look up to others;
most excellent, neither high nor low, I now pay homage to all the Kinsmen of the World.
He practices with equanimity toward gain and loss; like the moon among men, he causes the flowers of all marks to bloom.
Unstained by worldly dharmas as a lotus is by water, this Kinsman of the World can sever the branches of craving.
Having fully perfected the well-tamed mind and subdued it, With a mind of equanimity in generosity and precepts, free from anger;
The many difficult-to-subdue sentient beings have been largely tamed— O Well-Gone One, the moon among men, you who have subdued the mind.
His speech is soft, beautiful, and well-accordant with the mind; when he speaks, it can move the three thousandfold world system.
Gods, nāgas, asuras, humans, and others each think: "This is being said for me."
There is no nature of sentient beings—this is emptiness; there is no characteristic, and even aspiration is transcended.
The Honored One has taught that herein there is no place to go, nor is there any coming or dying.

The Dharma-realm is immovable and has no place of abiding; it does not cling to the past or the future, and in the interval between them, it is like empty space. The Honored One teaches this Dharma as being without conceptual thought.
The World-Honored One constantly speaks of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet within this, all worlds revolve in delusion.
Like the blind, they are filled with afflictions and anger, and they give rise to the thought:
"I" and "person."
This Dharma is like a phantom or a cloud; that which is seen by the eye is empty and motionless.
If one attains this supreme and wondrous patience, the Teachers will always follow them.

Just as various paintings are drawn upon the sky, Having no location and not abiding in any single place, so too does awakening abide naturally in such a manner; therefore, it has no likeness whatsoever in any single place.
All sounds, when heard, have no reality; they cannot be seen and have no place of abiding.
Whether heard or spoken, it is likewise so: their intrinsic nature is empty and immovable.
The Victorious One’s essential nature is likewise non-existent; one should see him as a manifestation like an illusion.
If one sees that his body is without conceptual differentiation, one should see the Sugata in this very same way.
All lands are equal; lands are not lands. All Buddhas are equal; so are the merits of the Buddhas.
All dharmas are equal; dharmas are empty and quiescent. All sentient beings are equal; there are no sentient beings.
That which is not exhausted is extinguished within exhaustion; that which is not exhausted is extinguished within the inexhaustible.
Whether it be exhaustion, non-exhaustion, or the exhaustion of non-exhaustion—this patience is thus ever-conforming.
Through conceptualization and further conceptualization, conceptualizations arise; yet all phenomena likewise have no place from which they arise.
If that which arises never actually arises, this patience thus constantly accords with it;
seeing seeing as always lacking the essence of seeing— if one sees in such a way as this,
and if these phenomena are empty and void, this patience thus constantly accords with it.

No one has ever been able to know the prior limit; because they do not know the supreme ultimate reality, if one knows that limits are eternally limitless, then that prior limit is accordingly severed.
Not relying on the finite or the infinite, never dwelling on this shore or the other shore;
if there is no place of abiding within the three realms of existence, then one dwells in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
If one dwells in the limit of reality, then there is no place of abiding within those three realms of existence.
If there is no place of abiding within the three realms of existence, one then dwells eternally within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
If form is seen as resembling a mass of foam upon water, and feeling is known to be like a bubble on the surface,
and perception is understood to be like a mirage— if one knows this, one dwells within the limit of reality.

All aggregates are inherently unstable conditioned phenomena; if one knows them to be like plantain trees and the like, and knows that the mind is similar to an illusion, then those aggregates, which are like murderers, are extinguished.
If one skillfully cultivates mindfulness toward loving-kindness and compassion, Without relying on either self or others,
and practices the supreme, pure conduct of mindfulness, That person shall become a Buddha like a pure celestial being;
If one is free from all pervasive afflictions, Then one will never again have any grasping or attachment.
Relinquishing all that one possesses without exception— such giving is praised by the Sugata.
If one perceives the body as being like the moon reflected in water, knows the path of speech to be like an echo in the mountains,
and understands the mind to be like lightning in the sky, then one’s morality is supreme within the three realms of existence.
If one has reached the further shore through patience and self-restraint, external circumstances cannot cause harm;
knowing the six sense faculties to be like an empty village, such patience is praised by the Sugata.
If one delights in solitude and is free from fear, the wise will frequent their sphere of activity.
With body and mind tranquil, practicing with pure integrity, they advance toward excellence within the three realms of existence.
If a person’s afflictions are extinguished by their very nature, and they are one of empty wisdom, free from conceptualization and serene,
and if their perceptions do not stir within the three realms of existence, they will surely be praised by the Sugata.
If one knows that herein there is no person, one shall attain supreme wisdom;
one should remain tranquil, free from conceptual proliferation, for that wisdom is preeminent within the three realms of existence.
If one does not grow weary amidst existence, then even the suffering endured while practicing throughout millions of eons [is transcended].
Never have I envied the inferior vehicles; the hosts of Māras are all struck with terror.
Just as one might take a drop of water from the great ocean, I have described only such a small measure of the most supreme virtues.
The Buddha-dharma is vast and boundless; its limits have never been reached.
"O King of Joy!

At that time, when the youth Dharmodgata spoke these verses before the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Ratnarcis-tejorāja, the entire trichiliocosm shook in six ways; hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of musical instruments were played simultaneously, and a rain of various perfumes, flower garlands, ointments, and powdered incense fell. Furthermore, eight thousand bodhisattvas all attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and King Ratnacandra, along with his women, children, and the great assembly, all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
“King of Joy!
At that time, the youth Dharmodgata addressed the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnārcis-tejo-rāja-cakra, saying:
‘Blessed One!...’”
What is the samādhi by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva shall be able to grasp all dharmas,
shall be able to grasp the meritorious adornments of buddha-fields, shall be able to fulfill the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas,
shall be able to obtain unsurpassed enjoyments and resources, and shall be able to transcend all māras and afflictions?

Because of the elimination of afflictions and evils, one shall attain the fulfillment of right mindfulness, right intention, and right conduct, as well as the abiding in shame, remorse, and sustaining wisdom;
one shall attain the gathering of all that has been heard; one shall attain the fulfillment of the superior knowledge of the five supernormal powers;
one shall attain the dhāraṇī of unattached eloquence; and one shall attain the fulfillment of eloquence.
Because they shall fulfill the six pāramitās; because they shall fulfill their birth, lineage, physical form, and enjoyments;
because they shall obtain pleasing speech and activities; because they shall fulfill all meritorious qualities;
because they shall attain perfect knowledge of entering and arising from various meditative absorptions, liberations, and samādhis; and because they shall attain fulfillment.

“Because he is fully endowed with all kinds of meritorious wisdom, why does he remain before you, performing the Buddha-work for the sake of sentient beings, even though he has not yet attained universal wisdom?
When this had been said, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Ratnārci-tejorāja-cakravartin, addressed the youth Dharmottara as follows:
“O youth! Listen well, listen well, and attend closely; I shall explain it for you.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with samādhi, they shall attain this, as well as other immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable supreme merits, and shall also swiftly proceed toward the site of enlightenment.”

"O youth! There is a samādhi called 'Proclaiming the Definitive Observation of the Practice of All Dharmas. Once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained this samādhi, they transcend all realms of Māra and shall swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Then that Tathāgata, for the sake of that youth, extensively explained this samādhi in verse:
“As one speaks, so one acts; having acted, one does not speak falsely.
With body, speech, and mind pure, one benefits others with a compassionate heart.”
Never forgetting compassion, and wearying of the practice of all desires,
one constantly and joyfully seeks the Dharma, never abandoning the vow of wisdom.
Amidst skillful speech, one enters the intelligence of sentient beings.
Do not be attached to bodily actions, nor harbor greed within the body.
One should abandon coarse and evil speech and refrain from mental proliferation.
Relieve those suffering beings and constantly awaken those who are heedless.
The diligent are taught what accords with the Dharma; those who regret are made to disperse [their thoughts].

Not dwelling on the notion of sentient beings, one does not differentiate between phenomena. Remaining far removed from grasping and rejection, [the verse in the Sanskrit original originally lacked one line: "one does not differentiate between the perception of things."
All marks should likewise be extinguished within the unmoving sphere of experience.
One should constantly seek wisdom and remain far removed from worldly discourse;
one should seek that which transcends the world, maintaining right mindfulness without forgetfulness.
Maintaining mindfulness toward all phenomena, one should thus be skillful;
with the fulfillment of one's practice, one should act in accordance with the ways of the world.
One should have faith in the ripening of karma and remain far removed from a lack of faith.
One should place faith in all Buddhas and maintain mindfulness of them accordingly;
one should constantly confess one's transgressions, rejoice in the accumulation of merit,
and likewise offer supplications to the Buddhas, prostrate, and dedicate the merit.
Always subdue pride, and practice virtue without satiety;
always remain diligently engaged, practicing repeatedly without negligence.
Having accomplished right practice, one should know that this is the cause of what is done.
Do not pursue the names established by convention; when rebuked, do not give rise to anger.
Do not cling to words, nor think of them as reality.
Seek not to dwell in the various realms of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
Just as one receives the retribution of one's karma, one should have faith in its results;
by sharing the goods one uses, one does not violate the teachings.
One should maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings and not harm even a single person.
Be neither diligent nor indolent, and do not give way to anger; do not envy what others have attained.
Fulfill whatever your heart desires, protect your vows in accordance with the Dharma, never abandon the precepts, and utterly eradicate pride.
Turning one's back on the fault of anger, One also uproots delusion;
Without giving rise to craving, One is content with whatever is obtained.
Having abandoned all kinsmen and acquaintances, The mind does not sink for lack of gain.
One should not be elated by gain, but rejoice only in the benefit of the Dharma.
Always distribute things with equanimity and remain free from hoarding.
When hearing harsh words, one should endure them and accept them with patience.
Always guard one's speech and preach the vehicle of Bodhi;
always exhort others toward diligent application and constantly associate with those who are energetic;
one should always inquire of the wise and further cultivate subtle, right concentration.
Do not abandon secluded lodgings; dwell with few desires and many needs.
One should have faith and understanding in emptiness, remaining unattached to worldly affairs.
Do not rely upon the assembly, nor be greedy for the elements.
Not perceiving an internal self, not being attached to sensory objects,
extinguishing all inverted thoughts, one should maintain constant mindfulness within the mind.
One should give rise to wisdom and always practice right conduct.
With a mind free from timidity or narrowness, one should contemplate the pure field of merit.
One should relinquish all conditioned activities; having given, one should harbor no expectation, nor dwell upon the observance of precepts, nor engage in discrimination regarding patience.
One should not initiate worldly diligence, nor rely upon meditative concentration;
one should not forget any phenomena, but should always awaken to wisdom.
One should enter into the various pāramitās, yet never harbor thoughts of one's own merits.
Hearing of others' virtues, one does not feel anger or malice; regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned, the mind remains equanimous.
Constantly taking nirvāṇa as its object of focus, one should always remain detached from the conditioned.
Knowing liberation and peace at all times, one regards the perception of the aggregates as being like that of a murderer.
Always cultivate love for the state of nirvana; dwell constantly in harmony and patience.
Maintain a smiling face and never frown; when seeing others, be the first to greet them with inquiry.
He shows loving respect toward the elders, and his mind and wisdom are constantly and skillfully sustained;
he never inflicts punishment upon others, and he brings all strife and contention to stillness.
One should always speak in praise of tranquility, Constantly teaching and harmonizing sentient beings;
Maintaining equanimity toward both the beloved and the unloved, One should always seek the gateway of dhāraṇī.
As a mother loves all sentient beings, as a father loves the assembly of noble ones,
as one loves those who are respected as if they were one's own recitation, so does one love the bodhisattvas as if they were Buddhas.
Love the Dharma as you love yourself; seek what you have heard without weariness or satiety.
Having heard the Dharma, practice it correctly, and always make offerings to the Tathāgata.
One should have faith and resolve in the supreme Dharma; without shame or timidity and without indolence, one should always make offerings to the Triple Gem and always endure improper speech.
Always without attachment to one's own body, nor craving for the duration of life;
maintaining a pure livelihood by constantly begging for alms, never abandoning the *dhuta* practices and always following the proper sequence.
Having long dwelt in seclusion and never departed from it, you should now leave your followers ever further and further away;
do not delight in dwelling together with householders, and do not become a confused and disorderly renunciant.
Do not be greedy, do not be deceitful, and begin with kind words; teach and transform many people so they enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
When preaching the Dharma, let your mind be free from timidity or small-mindedness; through skillful means, skillfully enter contemplation to know others.
One should repeatedly bring the Buddha to mind, Constantly contemplate the Dharma without negligence,
Always show respect toward the Saṅgha, And always make offerings to those who possess wisdom.

One should also constantly associate with those of skillful wisdom; always remain free from contention toward those in meditative concentration, and assist those who are diligent with a benevolent heart;
furthermore, one should mindfully cultivate the practice of faith and meritorious deeds.
To transform sentient beings and lead them to do good, those with faith should cherish love without crookedness;
if they encounter painful matters, they should be able to dispel them, always acting at the proper time and abandoning what is untimely.
Always practicing with fear and a sense of shame, one feels abashment and dread toward those evils;
having distanced oneself from all improper conduct, one constantly attends upon those who practice correctly.
Guarding the precepts for the sake of liberation, one should also seek noble conduct;
one should constantly practice the four foundations of mindfulness and always remain close to the four right efforts;
one should accomplish the bases of psychic power and give rise to the spiritual faculties.
One should seek power as one seeks meditative concentration, and constantly observe the seven factors of enlightenment;
one should always practice the Eightfold Path and also seek to gather *śamatha*;
*vipaśyanā* should constantly give rise to the truths, which the mind follows with sympathetic joy and observes.
Rejoicing in the Dharma, further joy arises; one should likewise transcend all objects of attachment.
Hearing that there is no place of abiding, do not be terrified; regarding that which cannot be grasped, do not be negligent.
One should always seek and aspire to the practice of Bodhi; one should cultivate faith and weigh the conduct of the Buddhas.
One should feel weary of and abandon the practice of sensory realms, and even within prior practices, one should likewise relinquish them.
Purify your own karma and do not speak ill of others; maintain the discipline of the Vinaya without breach at all times.
Train well in the prohibitions of the Prātimokṣa; always act according to the proper time and abandon what is untimely.
Skillfully able to deliberate upon what should be approached or departed from, knowing the measure of excellent things and restraining oneself,
being content with the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa), one likewise seeks to enter into supreme wisdom and supernormal powers.
Within samādhi one should take as an object of focus, and through the practice of concentration, know the entry;
one should enter according to the desires of the minds of sentient beings, following the words spoken by the Teacher.
One should also embrace the teaching of non-self; if one applies oneself with diligence, one will bring joy to others.
Just as the Supreme Being contemplated and practiced, one should always mindfully cultivate this samādhi.
Having heard and gained faith in the correct practice of the śrāvakas, one should train accordingly in the path of the pratyekabuddhas.
The lineage of all Buddhas destroys Māra; one should always seek this samādhi.
The initiation of supreme awakening arises from giving; it is the practice of non-retrogression, the conduct of the Buddhas, and the path traversed by the wise for many koṭis of eons.
This is the sphere of Dharma practice for those who have heard the ocean of teachings.

Those who revere this dharma of the realm, and who have faith and understanding that it is true wealth—this is the manifestation of the Buddha’s dwelling place; for those who seek the treasure within this treasury of dharma.
In this field, those seeking its fruit find it; for those scorched by afflictions, it is a pleasure garden;
for those who delight in upholding the Dharma, it is a grove; and for those with craving and views, it is meditative concentration (samādhi).
For those who seek the white dharmas, this Mother gives birth;
for those who desire something yet lack a support, they should bind and grasp the supreme and wondrous signs, and likewise arrange the various secondary marks according to their characteristics.
The adornments of the buddha-fields abide herein; herein one shall also attain all forms of dhāraṇī-retention.
From this, various [teachings] emerge in accordance with awakening—pure speech and words of truth.

They are also able to transcend the realm of Māra; having donned their armor long ago, they have slain the afflictions and subdued their reliance [upon them], thereby crushing all that is unwholesome.
Desiring to cause all virtues to blaze forth, and desiring to adorn one's prayers and aspirations, the many Māras shall not break this; even as it is being spoken, it remains inexhaustible.
This seeking for equality with all the world is not the improper teaching of the non-Buddhist masters;
it can transcend the Dharma of the Śrāvakas and serves as the condition for the excellence of the Pratyekabuddhas.
This is the sustaining power of the knowledge of all-knowledge;
it is that toward which sentient beings proceed, and it is that which can instruct others according to reality—this is the speech of a true friend at this chosen time.
For those with stainless faculties who universally seek this divine eye and the Dharma-eye, he is the one who seeks out the teacher of the Dharma;
for those seeking the torch, he is the kindled flame; for those seeking the true vow, he is the ultimate truth;
for those seeking the gift of wealth, he is renunciation; for those seeking liberation from views, he is diligent application.
Those who seek the concentration of joy possess this pure faith; those who wish to hear the ocean of Dharma possess this right practice;
those who seek the concentration of Maitreya possess this power; and those who wish to seek the path of Dharma have them as their masters.
For those who desire pure and wondrous adornment, To tame one's own mind is the basis for that Brahma-state;
Seeking the Dharma through skillful means with a joyful heart, And being non-retrogressive—this is their practice.
This is the destination reached by the practice of speech; it is for those who constantly contemplate wisdom and possess sharp faculties.
This is the preliminary work of skillful means—the banner of wisdom of that bull among men.
For those seeking victory, it is their bows; for those seeking selflessness, it is Nārāyaṇa;
for those heading toward omniscience, this is the path; and for those seeking sublime liberation, it is the equality of ethical discipline.
This is one whom the devas and others constantly prostrate to; this is one to whom the nāgas and others constantly scatter flowers;
and it is for the sake of humans that offerings are made. The yakṣas offer rare praises, hundreds of arhats likewise pay homage, and even the supreme Bodhisattvas extol them.

If the Tathāgatas and others, regarding what they themselves contemplate, desire to guard the faculties, they obtain those cities; those who abide in accordance with the Dharma are joined with skillful means, and those who rely upon meditative concentration attain them.
It causes those with doubts to shatter them; it causes all who are deluded to sever their confusion;
it causes the affliction of pride to be extinguished. For those wishing to cross to the other shore, it enables them to cross;
for those oppressed by the entanglements of illness, it is this excellent medicine; for those who are diseased, it is the true cure.
One who seeks the principle of desire should contemplate thus: to extract the poisonous arrows of the afflictions,
to roar the lion’s roar without fear in the midst of the assembly, and to seek to hear the Dharma from the Sugata—
this is the path for attaining nirvāṇa, which can sever all evil destinies.
Having equally transcended the three realms, he seeks this adornment of the land of merit;
through the vajra-like samādhi and his final birth upon the lion throne,
the sought-after merit is not lost here, and all that is desired is herein gathered.
It causes those who are constantly weary to yearn with thirst; it arouses the desire for vigor in those who lack it;
it establishes those who rely on objective conditions; and it restrains those who engage in divergent practices, causing them to abide [in the path].
This accomplishment consists in the essence of equality; this abandonment consists in removing pride and negligence regarding objects;
this relinquishment consists in letting go of grasping at objects through inverted perception; it is the universal knowledge that thoroughly knows all varieties.
For those seeking wisdom, this is its birth; for those seeking merit, this assembly is never lost;
it causes those dependent on the three realms of existence to sever their desires, and it leads those who seek awakening to be eternally free from signs.
All phenomena are empty throughout the three periods of time; having realized this, one does not abandon them.
Through skillful means and wisdom at all times, one acts for the sake of all worlds.
Alas for the Buddha-lineage! It is through the Buddha-wisdom that it proceeds.
Do not seek out the faults of those who preach the Dharma;
likewise, do not deceive or disparage those you perceive as unlearned.
Do not feel anger toward the preacher of the Dharma, but rather honor and attend closely to them.
When you hear the truth, know it as such; do not slander the wise.
When giving the Dharma, do not seek material gain; when teaching the Dharma, do not be stingy.
Listen to the Dharma with mutual respect, and let not the mind be distracted.
Explain the Dharma with all your heart; if you see one who desires it, do not cut off the gift of Dharma. Do not let other matters intervene;
when asked with patience and straightforwardness, explain the teaching to them.
If one sees with a malicious mind, you should practice patience therein;
remorse and doubt—these you must sever.
If you see those who have not yet attained the Path, preach the Path to them.
When contemplating this concentration, one easily attains the wisdom of the Buddha.
Whatever offerings one makes, do so before the teacher of the Dharma;
seek the noble eightfold path and let not the mind be distracted by other matters.
If there is the evil mind of contention and strife, one must always subdue that which is difficult to subdue;
if one desires to attain the bases of supernormal power (ṛddhipāda), one must rely upon mindfulness,
wisdom, and the sphere of practice.
For those seekers of the Dharma, they initiate that which is taught to them;
if they set out on the path to enlightenment, they manifest as millions of Buddhas dwelling in their respective lands, teaching and transforming all sentient beings.
If those are the Dharma-preachers, [they shall attain this].
This taste is the most excellent;
those who practice the *araṇa* [non-conflict] way and seek mastery in play let out the lion’s roar.
Such is the conduct of the wise, performed for the sake of praising nirvāṇa.
Thermal energy severed, there is coolness; this is the verse of non-falling.
The teaching on the benefit of liberation brings joy and bliss arising in the body, and the mind is likewise filled with wonder and delight; the wise one sports in wisdom.
Seeking all-encompassing wisdom, they have pure faith in these teachings;
abiding in the non-retrogressive Buddha-wisdom, they are certain of enlightenment.
Cultivating the perfuming of pure dharmas, they shall abandon all evils.
When one eliminates what is dark, the white dharma naturally arises.
For those who train in the precepts and seek merit, this will be accomplished for them;
if they so desire, it shall correspond to their aim.
They have attained within this body the marks of supreme beauty;
the Buddha knows this conduct as it truly is, having been approached by all the noble ones.
Within the wisdom that illuminates wisdom, they have attained the Buddha-wisdom and universal wisdom.
Having dwelt here, one shall behold millions of exquisite lands.
Therein, that One of Great Power, the Wise One, shall answer the doubts that are asked;
having severed all these doubts, all delusions will be abandoned and extinguished.
Within this, the Buddha-dharma arises, praised by the supreme person;
one abandons all evils of the world and every defilement of the afflictions.
Without losing any merit, if one desires to seek blessings, [one should practice here].
Those wise ones take the Dharma as their supreme object;
they delight in this eye of the Dharma, and draw near to those who are fierce and courageous.
Desiring eloquent speech, they approach the fountain of the Dharma, the treasury of discernment.
Having already explained their protection, as well as all those who preach the Dharma,
the various causes and conditions for wisdom, and those who rely on craving and views;
[I shall now explain] how to skillfully act within all phenomena regarding both harmony and disharmony.
Having explained the divisions of the essence of wisdom and skillful means regarding all phenomena,
one thus manifests all phenomena through the contemplation of true wisdom;
therein, severing the net of craving, one should abandon all attachments.
When ignorance is dispersed therein, clarity shall manifest before one;
therein, one universally knows the enumerations, and what he speaks is without attachment.
Having extensively explained the various minds of wisdom and intention herein, [he remains unattached].
Grasping at form and name, they speak of these within;
observing the domain of the six sense bases as if seeing an empty village,
one who knows the external through contact shall behold the Buddha-wisdom.
If one is free from the three kinds of speech, those [beings] take hold therein;
and when the three kinds of craving are extinguished, they speak of that therein.
In that state, they speak of relinquishment; wherever that which is produced arises, [they speak of it].
They have severed existence; this is taught within this meditative concentration.
Birth and illness are cut off, and they are free from the poisoned arrow of death.
Within it, all sufferings are stilled, as are the various streams of conceptual proliferation.
It brings joy to all who are sorrowful and dissolves all evil intentions;
it accomplishes pure skillful means for those who practice that Dharma.
It brings fulfillment to those who observe with discernment and to all who seek excellence.
Bringing light amidst hatred and evil, when there is any delusion of the eye;
here the Buddha’s thunder resounds as he turns the wheel of Dharma.
When Vajrapāṇi proclaims this, it is like the wisdom of that world.
Within this, all turbid and chaotic afflictions are universally washed away;
within this, all views are destroyed, as well as whatever bases there may be for the self.
Receiving, grasping, and maintaining—all these have already been explained herein.
It is well; within the wisdom of the Buddha, one shall thus attain victory.
Constantly increasing all dharmas—this is the path of skillful wisdom.
The pure dharmas are ever accumulated, remaining far removed from all evil karma.
Constantly contemplate and cultivate the Buddha-dharma; When speaking, be free from stinginess.
Do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas, But abide firmly within it.
The lineage of the Dharma blazes brightly, And the noble assembly can universally embrace it.
One should subdue all masters of treatises and those non-Buddhists who seek to arise.
When they praise the teaching, saying "Excellent!", one should respond with such words;
yet while constantly practicing the conduct of awakening, one should maintain a mind free from attachment toward them.
Toward all sentient beings, be like the moon, always maintaining a friendly disposition;
toward all phenomena, be like the sun, constantly upholding right reflection.
Always regarding them as teachers, one should contemplate this meditative concentration therein.
This concentration is like a king; for the sake of sentient beings, it is extensively expounded.
It is the guide for the wise; through pure dharmas and right faith in the mind, it ripens the fruit of ambrosia and causes one to remember past lives.
Conception without defilement, The rejection of the ways of foolish children—
These are the virtues of the Great Sage Buddha, Whose praise is boundless.
When upholding the wisdom of the Buddha, And when reciting what the Sugata has spoken,
When one writes it with wisdom, or speaks it, one shall obtain merit.
Far removed from all non-Buddhists, this is the immovable state;
that which is spoken is received by the world, as taught by all the Buddhas.
The merits of the Buddhas of the past, the aspirations for the future,
and the Buddhas dwelling in the present— these are the various treasuries of jewels.
To cause sentient beings to enter the practice, they preach the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Not forgetting wisdom—this is the seal of the Buddha-dharma.
This emerges from that which is fierce and powerful; this jewel is unchanging and brings about the swift attainment of all knowledges. Thus one desires to inquire into the virtues of the Buddha.
One who is never satiated with the phenomena of desire shall scatter the fires of all afflictions and attain the wisdom of skillful means;
they shall enter the water-element and enter the fire-element concentration.
The wind element has no place of abiding; the space element is without delusion.
Within the manifestation of the wisdom-element, they cause entry into the dharma-realm;
causing weariness with all conditioned formations, they cause the dispersal of all attachments and defilements.
Hating the ocean of all existences, He eliminates the affliction of all defilements;
Causing others to relinquish all phenomena, He skillfully knows through his own discernment.
He also skillfully knows the conduct of others, And his desire to speak is inexhaustible.
Within skillful means there is no turbidity; one should understand how to act accordingly in both leaving home and remaining in the world.
One should abandon the view of self and distance oneself from "mine-ness.
Attachment should be cast away, and pride should always be subdued.
For food, act like a dog; in giving, be moderate and free from greed.
Eat until you are fully satisfied, and once finished, know that there is joy.
Do not be destitute while in the shade; cross the great waters with haste.
Unbreakable by any treatises, pure and straightforward, free from objective clinging;
Distant from sleep, drawing near to those who preach the Dharma;
Transcending restlessness and playfulness, one should likewise extinguish doubt.
And cause the dispersal of all desires, while also remaining far removed from indolence.
Not perceiving a locus for a self, one makes non-self manifest;
not abiding in a "living being," one should likewise not come into contact with phenomena.
Within the Dharma free from strife, one speaks with impartiality on what is meaningful;
with a mind of skillful reflection, one realizes that all conditioned phenomena are non-existent.
One should draw near to the wise and remain undaunted in all circumstances.
Within that, one should have faith and understanding; amidst the assembly, do not be afraid.
One should speak of the virtues of others and not exalt oneself.
One should always practice that which is the sphere of activity of the All-Knowing One.
Do not be attached to or dwell upon your dwelling place; you should depart like a flying bird.
Do not act for the sake of gain and offerings, nor should you harbor thoughts of your own self.
Let your mind be neither diminished nor inferior, and skillfully know the proper places for walking meditation.
One should practice with mindfulness in accordance with the Dharma; do not think, nor do you recall.
One should also seek liberation; one should always remain in a quiet place, constantly mindful of practicing the holy life, and shall swiftly attain meditative concentration.
With loving-kindness toward an impartial mind, with compassion one should gather others in;
taking joy as the delight in the Dharma, one should practice equanimity where it is appropriate.
Through precepts, have pity for others; through concentration, one should awaken to the Dharma.
Acting with wisdom in what ought to be done, one will have no regret or distress later.
One should bring forth inexhaustible knowledge and likewise employ skillful speech;
I say that one should enter into discourse, yet when speaking, do not seek profit.
Do not delight in various kinds of idle talk; this is to abide without weariness.
Neither abandoning nor grasping—these dharmas are bodhi.
Do not destroy or annihilate any dharmas; thus has it been clearly explained.
Do not deceive sentient beings; you should take refuge in the Three Jewels.
You should embrace the True Dharma and make firm your vows;
do not envy the Lesser Vehicle, but apply yourself with diligence day and night.
"For the sake of seeking all dharmas, it is from this that omniscience arises;
for all Buddhas, this is a treasury, and their samādhis are like the ocean.
"O King of Joy!"

At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnaprabhā-tejomaṇḍala-rāja extensively expounded for the youth Dharmottara this samādhi called "The Definitive Observation of All These Dharma Practices" by means of verses.

When he taught this samādhi, King Ratnacandra and his sons and retinue attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; one thousand sentient beings fulfilled their resolve for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and immeasurable sentient beings increased in their training on the stages.
“Rājavikrīḍita, do you think that the youth named Dharmodgata at that time and on that occasion was someone else?
Do not hold such a divergent view.
Why is this? Son of good family, you are that very Kāla; you are the one named Dharma-uttara, the youth of the Samaya.
Son of good family!
He who was King Ratnacandra at that time and in that kalpa is none other than the present Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya;
and those who were his princes at that time and in that kalpa are these very members of the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas now seated here.

“King Priya! At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, together with his parents, elders, friends, and acquaintances—totaling thirty-six thousand koṭis of sentient beings—left the household life for homelessness within the teaching of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Ratnarcis-cakravartin.”
O King of Joy!
There are many who, out of love and devotion for the teaching of that Blessed One, have become bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood this meaning and wishing to further clarify it beyond measure, spoke these verses:
"I recall many koṭis of kalpas ago, There was a most excellent one named Ratnaprabha;
His assembly of monks was likewise vast and numerous, Consisting of those whose outflows were exhausted as well as bodhisattvas."
That land is pure and lovely, naturally adorned like a celestial palace;
its cities, villages, and gardens are magnificent, strewn with flowers as level as the palm of a hand.
In that realm there was a king named Ratnacandra, a sovereign lord over many thousands of continents;
endowed with merit and wisdom, he was a wise man whose boundless treasuries possessed vast supernormal powers.
He delights in sporting within the groves; a celestial wife cradles a newborn boy named Dharmottara, who is most beautiful to behold, adorned with a supreme gathering of golden hues.
Immediately upon his birth, he spoke sublime words, praising the Buddha’s Dharma,
as well as the faults of household life and the virtues of solitude, and he also extensively expounded upon the transgressions of sensual desires.
He transformed his parents and kinsmen, saying:
"The wise should reflect and cause their faith to be pure.
The king, filled with joy and leaping for gladness, set out toward the presence of the most excellent Great Sage.

The youth no longer entered his home; instead, right there in that garden, together with his father, his relatives and acquaintances, and a great multitude—three hundred and sixty million beings—he approached the Buddha.
When that Great Elephant King had arrived, the Dharma King Ratnaprabha beheld him;
with a heart overflowing with joy and supreme affection, he prostrated at his feet and sat before him.
Dharmodgata also paid homage at the feet of the Most Excellent One; grasping his ten fingers, he joined his palms.
Having thus shown such reverence to that Honored One, the youth sang these verses in gāthā.
He extensively praised the supreme virtues and the true nature of all phenomena of the Teacher;
the king, his sons, and their retinue, having heard this, resolved their minds upon awakening.
Dharmodgata questioned the World-Honored One:
"You have spoken of this tranquil samādhi, free from all dust; by dwelling powerfully in this samādhi, one realizes awakening and subdues Māra."

The Honored One among bipeds, having understood the invitation and knowing that the youth’s mind was pure and full of faith, immediately taught him this concentration difficult to behold; the one of great majesty then sang these verses.
That Honored One taught this samādhi, wherein the bodhi of all Buddhas is free from dust and tranquil;
the king, along with his sons, ministers, and subjects, immediately abided in the Buddha-wisdom and became non-retrogressive.
There, many who were learners (śaikṣa) and those beyond learning (aśaikṣa) likewise heard of this tranquil concentration.
Furthermore, many other beings by the millions, Inspired by the thought of enlightenment, resolved their minds upon it.
The King, his sons, and their retinues Were all made to feel weary of and detached from the merits of the five desires;
At that time, with the youth as their leader, They abandoned this home and went forth into homelessness.
All those who cherish and delight in the Teacher fill the realms of gods and humans;
among the vast multitude of that Sugata’s followers, it is difficult to find even a measure of their number.
O King of Joy!
In times past, you were that youth named Dharmodgata;
and he who was the father-king at that time is now this very Bodhisattva Maitreya.
All those princes who existed at that time are these very members of the assembly gathered here;
sentient beings always abide within the realm of continuity, and having realized this, they are led toward pure conduct.
Therefore, having heard of this tranquil concentration, one should receive it with constant pure faith;
always explain it to others without stinginess, and the wisdom of a Buddha will not be difficult to attain.

The measure of that merit is not easily grasped; even if one were to speak for many millions of kalpas, if one can maintain this supreme samādhi, one should preach it for the sake of the multitude without negligence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva King of Joy addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
This samādhi brings about great benefit, for it is able to cause all the meritorious dharmas of the bodhisattvas to arise.”
"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva wishes to attain this samādhi, what dharmas should they draw near to, what should they practice with mindfulness, and what should they cultivate extensively?"
"What dharmas should one not associate with, should not cultivate through mindfulness, and should not practice frequently?
Excellent, World-Honored One!
What are these dharmas?"
"What kind of dharmas are absent?
Bhagavān, we pray that you will explain this in detail."
Sugata! I pray that you will analyze this for me:
what dharmas does a bodhisattva possess?
"What dharma is non-existent?
The Buddha said,
"O King of Joy!"
The bodhisattva is free from weariness amidst the cycle of existence; the bodhisattva makes no distinctions among sentient beings;
the bodhisattva does not grasp at material wealth; the bodhisattva is never partial in giving;
the bodhisattva is never lacking in reverence for training; in maintaining the precepts, there is no place of birth [for affliction]; and the mind is without...
Free from feverish distress, his mind is without cowardice; he is free from false thoughts and performs no actions without reflection;
among sentient beings, he harbors no intent to kill; regarding the wealth of others, he commits no theft;
regarding the wives of others, he has no lustful attachment; his verbal karma is not evil, and he utters no divisive speech.
There is harsh speech, yet no frivolous talk; no greed for the wealth of others;
no following after anger; no dense forest of views; no transgression regarding love for awakening;
no disparagement of the Dharma; no deception or pride toward the Saṅgha; no lack of reverence for the Honored Ones; and no fear regarding the gates of liberation.
He is untiring in performing deeds for others; he does not praise himself nor disparage others;
he does not conform to the process of saṃsāra, yet he does not fail to conform to that which is beyond saṃsāra;
the vows he has undertaken never waver or fall away; what he has already accomplished he never again undermines; and he understands the deeds performed by others.
One should act with gratitude and not seek anything for oneself; among those who are weak, one should not practice deception or oppression;
among those who have not yet studied, one should not treat them with contempt; one should not be attached to wife or children and should be free from love and hatred;
toward teachers, one should harbor no secrets; regarding the Dharma, one should act as a teacher without concealment; and among all phenomena, one should have no thought of harm or destruction.
They are without weariness in the giving of the Dharma; they are without indolence or fatigue in seeking the Dharma;
they do not preach for the sake of being bound by gain; they do not seek friendship through material gifts; they do not serve others with flattery; they are free from double-tongued speech;
they do not approach and serve others with deceitful delusion; and they do not harbor malice toward the Dharma.
Being without the notion of self or what belongs to self, not being attached to the body, not craving life, having no view of a self, harboring no enmity,
neither slandering the real nor the unreal, feeling no anger toward those subject to the laws of decline,
not loving for a short time, not betraying friends, and not deceiving those entrusted with one’s kin.
Not raising false accusations against those who are truthful or untruthful; not using falsehood as proof; not dismissing others at an improper time;
having no thought of contention or rivalry toward other sentient beings; being without indolence in initiating virtuous deeds;
not diminishing one’s patience; not retaliating with harsh words; not binding oneself to resentment; and not deceiving those who are lowly. Following...
He speaks with playful words free from envy; among the exquisite, he never abandons anything;
regarding food, he never fails to share it; when giving, he does not use inferior things;
toward women, he commits no misconduct; toward men, he has no defilement; he does not abandon right faith; and he trains in the precepts.
They are not lax; they possess a sense of shame and a dread of blame; they lack no small measure of merit or learning;
they feel no regret after giving; they are unerring in wisdom; they hold nothing but reverence for the Three Jewels;
they do not regard worldly conventions as solid; and they have no attachment to entering into ultimate truth.
There is no dense forest of views and conduct; there is no grasping at a self, yet right mindfulness is never forgotten; there is no divergent activity within the right abandonments;
there is no intoxication or relish within the bases of psychic power; the faculties are not weak and the powers are not feeble;
there is no lack of knowledge regarding the factors of enlightenment; there is no inversion regarding the path; and there is samādhi.
Within the middle there is no attachment to signs; within *śamatha* there is no fixed dwelling; within *vipaśyanā* there is no conceptualization;
within luminous liberation there is no contact or realization; within the truths there is no obstruction;
in crossing to the other shore there is nothing that is not initiated; one does not cling to the aggregates, nor to the elements.
Relying [on these], one does not obtain [them] at improper times; among the śrāvakas, there is no one who has witnessed a hundred [such instances].
Among all bodhisattvas, there is none who is not a teacher; regarding the sense bases, there is no mental conceptualization;
regarding all objects, there is no dependence; one is not born in the evil destinies due to one's own karma; and regarding dwelling in the womb...
Therein is no suffering or affliction; within the cycle of transmigration there is no joy or pleasure; within the cycle of transmigration there is no perception of suffering;
regarding all forms of deliverance there is no fear or dread; regarding all sentient beings, none are not fields [of merit];
there is not even a small amount of seed [to be sown]; regarding the place where one plants, one never harbors expectations; and regarding all fields of merit...

The recipient is without deficiency; one is not bound by limitations in giving, nor bound by limitations in upholding the precepts, nor bound by limitations in patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom; one is not bound by limitations in the cycle of transmigration;
loving-kindness is uninterrupted, great compassion is impartial, and there is no pride of attachment to a home.
...no pride in wealth, no pride in physical beauty, no pride in power, no pride in retinue,
no pride in extensive learning, no pride in maintaining the precepts, no pride in dwelling in seclusion,
no pride in having many virtues and few desires, no pride in [one's own] pride, and no anger or delusion...
He possesses latent tendencies toward craving; he does not regard perversions as real, nor does he regard the pure and the impure as dual;
he does not envy rebirth in the heavens, nor does he delight in sensual desires; he never associates with those who do not share his practice;
there is nothing he does not diligently apply himself to; he does not uphold worldly discourses; and among those of external paths, there is none for whom he does not feel compassion.
They have no conceptual fetters regarding phenomena; they do not seek their own pleasure;
they are free from feigned affection; and they do not rely upon Māra.
O King of Joy!
"The vows undertaken by all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shall never be shifted or slackened, continuing until they reach the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)," [said the Buddha] up to verse 150,
"O King of Joy!"
All these things belonging to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are non-existent; as for all other things that cannot be produced, one should not produce them.
Among these, what is there that can be produced?
O King of Joy!
All bodhisattvas should not slander others; they themselves should not slander others, but should attain stability for themselves.
In all their undertakings, they should be neither wavering nor lax; they should take up the heavy burden and should not engage in dark deeds.
In accordance with what is done, one should bring benefit to white (wholesome) deeds; within limited practices, one should achieve transcendence;
within immeasurable practices, one should likewise have already entered; regarding the moisture of affection, one should practice detachment;
regarding the measure of the Dharma, one should not be detached from it; regarding the suffering of birth and death, one should attain liberation; and regarding all births...
Because of reflecting upon the middle way, one will not fail to attain liberation; one will not take up unwholesome karma, but shall instead take up all roots of goodness;
regarding the giving of afflictions, the bodhisattva shall practice stinginess; regarding the giving of the Dharma, the bodhisattva shall not be stingy or parsimonious;
regarding the studies of non-Buddhists, one shall not practice or study them; and regarding that which is taught by the Buddhas...
One should practice the training with skill regarding what is permitted; one should practice non-forbearance regarding the forbearance of unequal views;
one should fulfill forbearance regarding the forbearance of right view; one should practice indolence regarding evil deeds;
one should arouse diligence regarding virtuous deeds; and one should forget mindfulness regarding birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Among the playful mastery of the five supernormal powers, one should find the flavor of meditative concentration; regarding the terrifying incantations of the *vetāla* and sorcery, one should regard them as a lack of wisdom;
and within supramundane knowledge, one should cultivate true wisdom.
"One should be like the moon, because one’s pure qualities (*śukladharma*) increase through an impartial mind toward all sentient beings;
one should be like the sun, because one dispels darkness and creates the light of wisdom;
one should be like the earth, because one remains impartial toward all sentient beings by being free from duality."
One should be like water, for it has no aversion toward impurities, whether pure or foul;
one should be like fire, for it burns away all afflictions;
one should be like wind, for it is unattached to any phenomena.
One should be like space, because of immeasurable wisdom;
one should be like the ocean, because of never being satiated in seeking roots of goodness;
one should be like Mount Meru, because of being invincible to all other teachers of doctrines.
One should be like a lotus flower, because one is unstained by the eight worldly dharmas;
one should be like a tree, because one is free from conceptual discrimination;

one should be like a seed-lineage, because the Dharma is inexhaustible, because all afflictions cannot trample upon it, because among the practices of sentient beings one should proceed toward them yet remains unattached to the various realms of existence, and because one should be directed toward Nirvana.
It should be regarded as a fertile field, for it removes the thorns of anger and resentment;
one should skillfully cultivate faith, as it is the foundation for practice;
and it shall yield great fruit, for it proclaims the Four Noble Truths.
One shall obtain great benefit, because of being within the Buddha-dharma;
one shall obtain freedom from hindrances, because of [attaining] wisdom, liberation, samādhi, and samāpatti;
one shall obtain joy, because of the joy of the Dharma.
One shall attain transcendence, for one has already crossed out of the mire of the sufferings of birth and death;
one shall fall into accord, through skillful means;
and one shall perform wholesome deeds, having become detached from what is discordant.
One should practice virtuous patience, because it pertains to realization;
one should practice pleasant speech, because of internal pure faith;
and one should act as a steadfast friend even unto nirvāṇa, because one is the most excellent of friends.
One should be pure and sincere, for there is no delusion;
one should be honest and straightforward, for there is no flattery or crookedness;
one should be gentle and flexible, for it is easy to dwell together with others.
One should regard it as delightful, because it internally moistens faith;
one should regard it as reaching all places, because it turns in accordance [with conditions];
one should regard it as being moistening, because of great compassion.
One should feel thirsty for the site of enlightenment;
one should not thirst for various sensual desires;
and one should cause the śrāvakas to be fully satisfied.
One should practice instruction for the sake of all pratyekabuddhas;
one should practice mindfulness for the sake of all roots of goodness;
and one should practice awakening amidst unwholesome states.
One should act as a guardian for the sake of the True Dharma;
one should act so as not to sever the lineage of the Triple Gem;
and one should act with fervor for the sake of all wholesome dharmas.
"O King of Joy!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should bring all evil karma to cessation.
O King of Joy!"
To speak briefly, unwholesome dharmas do not exist for Bodhisattvas;
all conditioned phenomena and wholesome dharmas should be said to exist.
In this way, you should train yourselves; such is my instruction.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King of Joy (Nandirāja) was filled with delight, as were all the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who had gathered from the various directions, along with the great assembly of devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others. Upon hearing what the Buddha had taught, there was none who did not rejoice; they leaped for joy beyond measure and venerated him with diligent offerings, all greatly rejoicing in what the Buddha had spoken.
